title: Sharing charge in three contacts
steps: Call the original charge Q. After contact 1–2, the charges are Q/2, Q/2, 0.
After contact 2–3, they are Q/2, Q/4, Q/4.
After contact 3–1, they are 3Q/8, Q/4, 3Q/8, so Q1 = Q3 > Q2.
pitfall: Average only the two spheres that actually touch at each step.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A grounded charge reservoir
steps: The first contact makes spheres 1 and 2 equally positive.
Sphere 2 then touches grounded sphere 3. With no nearby external influence, electrons arrive from Earth until both are neutral.
Sphere 1 stays isolated and positive: Q1 > Q2 = Q3 = 0.
pitfall: Ground is a source or sink of electrons, not an insulating connection.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Rubbing transfers electrons
steps: The two-sphere system started with zero net charge.
X ends at −5 nC, so Y must end at +5 nC by charge conservation.
Y lost electrons to X; protons remain bound in nuclei.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Keep a running charge ledger
steps: The figure gives A = +1 μC, B = +5 μC, C = +3 μC.
After A and B touch, B has (1+5)/2 = 3 μC.
After B and C touch, B remains (3+3)/2 = 3 μC. Thus Q0 > Q1 = Q2.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

steps: Initially

Total charge is −Q, so each identical sphere ends at −Q/2.
The final repulsive force has magnitude kQ²/(4d²), one eighth of the original.
pitfall: Do not average the magnitudes; conserve signed charge.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Grounding a conductor versus an insulator
steps: A negative rod repels mobile electrons in the grounded conductor into Earth.
The conducting sphere therefore gains net positive charge, Qc > 0.
In the ideal insulating sphere charges cannot flow freely to ground; polarization leaves approximately Qi = 0. Hence Qc > Qi.
pitfall: Polarization and net charging are different processes.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Order of induction matters
steps: Bring the positive cube near the neutral sphere (2), attracting electrons toward the cube.
Connect ground (4): extra electrons enter. Remove the ground connection while the cube is still present (5).
Finally remove the cube (3). The trapped excess electrons leave a negative sphere.
pitfall: If the cube leaves before ground is disconnected, the extra electrons can leave again.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Induced negative charge
steps: The nearby positive rod attracts electrons.
While grounded, electrons flow from Earth onto the sphere.
Disconnecting ground traps those electrons; removing the rod redistributes them but does not remove the net negative charge.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Two grounding sequences
steps: Both positive rods initially attract electrons from Earth onto their spheres.
Sphere 1 is disconnected while its rod remains: excess electrons are trapped.
Sphere 2 stays grounded while its rod is removed: excess electrons return to Earth. Final states are negative and neutral, respectively.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Charge transferred is the change
steps: The conserved total is +1 nC − 3 nC = −2 nC.
Identical spheres share this equally, ending at −1 nC each.
The first sphere changes by −2 nC, so the transferred magnitude is 2 nC: half the initial charge difference.
pitfall: The final charge is not the transferred charge; compare initial and final states.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A neutral wall can attract
steps: The negative balloon slightly displaces bound electrons in the wall away from it.
The nearer side of the wall becomes slightly positive and the farther side slightly negative.
Because the attractive positive charge is closer, attraction exceeds repulsion and the balloon can stick.
pitfall: An insulator can polarize without conducting charge away.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A ground connection permits induction
steps: The positive insulating sphere attracts electrons in the conductor.
The ground wire provides a path for extra electrons to enter sphere 2.
Sphere 2 gains net negative charge even though the spheres never touch.
pitfall: Grounding does not force an object to remain electrically neutral near an external charge.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Surface field and radius
steps: Outside an isolated spherical conductor, E = kQ/r².
At the surface, put r equal to the sphere radius.
Esmall/Elarge = R²/(R/2)² = 4.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cancel the field at the origin
steps: At O, +2q at +3a produces a leftward field 2kq/(9a²); +q at −3a produces rightward kq/(9a²).
The existing net field is leftward kq/(9a²). A positive extra charge must be on the left to oppose it.
Set 4kq/x² = kq/(9a²), giving
x
= 6a and x = −6a.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Same density means more total charge
steps: For uniform density, Q = ρ(4πR³/3).
At the surface E = kQ/R² = ρR/(3ε0).
Doubling R at fixed density doubles E.
pitfall: Do not treat Q as fixed when density and radius are specified.
integration: Q(R) = ∫₀ᴿ ρ4πr² dr = 4πρR³/3; substitute into Gauss’s law.

title: Electric force follows charge sign
steps: The force is F = qE.
A proton has positive charge, so its force points in the same direction as E.
The answer is +y; its initial +x velocity does not change the electric-force direction.
pitfall: The velocity cross-product rule belongs to magnetic force, not electric force.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Fields add between opposite charges
steps: At B, midway between +3 μC and −3 μC, both field contributions point from positive to negative.
Each contribution has magnitude k
Q
/d², so the total is 2k
Q
/d².
At the outer points the fields oppose, and at off-axis points vector components reduce the total. Thus B is strongest.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Resolve the three contributions
steps: At B, the nearby negative sphere pulls the field to the left.
The two lower positive spheres contribute upward components.
The nearby negative sphere dominates the horizontal balance, while the positive spheres give the net upward component: left and up.
pitfall: At A, C, and D left-right symmetry forces the horizontal component to zero.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Smallest rightward field
steps: Between +4Q and −3Q, both fields point right.
Using one tick spacing as a, B gives 4 + 3/16, C gives 4/9 + 3/4, and D gives 4/16 + 3 in units kQ/a².
C has the smallest of these rightward magnitudes; A and E have leftward fields.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Zero field outside opposite charges
steps: Between opposite charges their fields point in the same direction, so cancellation is impossible there.
Outside the pair, cancellation lies on the side of the smaller magnitude, +Q.
At A the distance to −4Q is twice the distance to +Q, making kQ/r² = k(4Q)/(2r)².
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Off-axis field of unequal charges
steps: P is equally far from +Q and −4Q.
The positive charge contributes up and right; the negative charge contributes down and right with four times the magnitude.
Horizontal contributions add rightward, and the larger downward component wins: +x and −y.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cancellation at a midpoint
steps: Equal distances mean equal field magnitudes require equal charge magnitudes.
At a midpoint, same-sign charges produce opposing field directions.
Therefore the charges must have equal magnitudes and the same sign.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A dipole in a spreading field
steps: The positive end feels force along the local field; the negative end feels force opposite the field.
The pair of forces turns the dipole clockwise toward alignment.
Field lines are closer at the positive, left end, so its rightward force is stronger: the net force is toward the right.
pitfall: A nonuniform field can exert both torque and net force on a neutral dipole.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Use the missing corner
steps: Four equal positive charges at all four corners would give zero field at the center.
The top-right and bottom-left charges cancel each other.
The remaining top-left charge pushes a positive test charge down and right, toward the missing corner: option E.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Electric levitation
steps: Equilibrium means upward electric force balances downward weight Mg.
Magnitude
Felec
= QE, so QE = Mg.
E = Mg/Q. Because the particle is negative, the field itself points downward.
pitfall: Height D is irrelevant in the near-Earth uniform-g model.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Reposition an opposite charge
steps: Initially the positive charge is d from P and the negative charge is 2d away: Ei = kQ/d² − kQ/(4d²) = 3kQ/(4d²).
Finally both charges are distance d from P, and both fields point right: Ef = 2kQ/d².
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Use source-to-observation distances
steps: Both positive spheres are to the left of x3, so both fields point right.
The distances are x3−x1 and x3−x2, not the source coordinates themselves.
Add the magnitudes: E = k[q1/(x3−x1)² + q2/(x3−x2)²].
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Field lines at conductor surfaces
steps: Lines leave the positively charged inner sphere and end on induced negative charge on the cavity wall.
In electrostatic equilibrium, the field must be perpendicular to both conducting surfaces.
Because the sphere is off-center, the lines bend to meet both surfaces normally; option C satisfies these requirements.
pitfall: Straight radial rays from the small sphere generally strike the offset outer wall obliquely.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A midpoint field grows by one half
steps: Initially the two equal and opposite charges give equal fields pointing in the same direction.
Call each contribution e, so E = 2e.
Doubling the positive charge makes the new field 2e+e = 3e = 3E/2.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Add opposite-charge midpoint fields
steps: Each sphere is d/2 from the midpoint.
The +3Q and −Q fields point the same way there, so E = k(3Q+Q)/(d/2)² = 16kQ/d².
Using k = 1/(4πε0) gives E = 4Q/(πε0d²).
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Inside and outside a conductor
steps: Free charges rearrange until E = 0 everywhere inside the metal.
Outside an isolated spherical conductor, E = k
Q
/r².
This decreases toward zero as r grows, but is nonzero at every finite external distance.
pitfall: Approaching zero is different from reaching zero at a finite distance.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Keep the same force ratio
steps: Resolve tension: T sinθ = qE and T cosθ = mg, so tanθ = qE/(mg).
On the Moon g becomes g/6, so q/m must become one sixth its former value if E is unchanged.
Tripling m and halving q gives (q/2)/(3m) = (q/m)/6, preserving the angle.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cancellation between like charges
steps: Outside the pair the fields point the same way, so they cannot cancel.
Between charges the fields oppose.
The zero is nearer the smaller charge +Q, so its smaller charge is compensated by a shorter distance.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Suspend a negative object
steps: Balance requires
q
The force must point upward, so the field must point downward because q is negative.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Opposite pairs cancel
steps: For every charge on the circle, there is an equal charge diametrically opposite it.
Their fields at the center have equal magnitudes and opposite directions.
Three such pairs give a net field of zero.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Horizontal addition in a square
steps: The two +2Q charges on the left push the field rightward at P.
The two −Q charges on the right also pull the field rightward.
For each vertical pair the vertical components cancel, leaving a purely rightward field: E.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A dipole at an equilateral vertex
steps: The fields from +Q and −Q have equal magnitude kQ/a².
Their vertical components are opposite and cancel.
Both horizontal components point from +Q toward −Q, to the right.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Compare two dipole locations
steps: At O the fields add: E = 2kq/d².
At N, distances to +q and −q are 3d and d. The stronger negative-charge field points left.
EN = kq/d² − kq/(9d²) = (8/9)kq/d² = 4E/9, leftward.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Read field-line density
steps: Field strength is represented by how closely neighboring field lines are packed.
Near A, next to sphere 1, the lines are most crowded of the labeled positions.
Therefore the largest magnitude is at A.
pitfall: Do not confuse the number labeling a sphere with a field-strength ranking.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A spherical capacitor field
steps: The inner conductor is −Q and the surrounding shell is +Q.
Field lines point inward across the gap, from positive shell to negative sphere.
There is no field inside the metal, and the total exterior enclosed charge is zero. Option B shows only inward gap lines.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Two tiny charges at a midpoint
steps: The midpoint is 0.10 m from each charge.
Each field has magnitude k(2.0×10⁻¹⁷)/(0.10)² = 1.8×10⁻⁵ N/C.
The opposite signs make the fields add: total 3.6×10⁻⁵ N/C.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cancel horizontal components
steps: For A, EA,x = k(2.0 nC)/2² × cos60°.
For B, EB,x = kqB/(√6)² × cos45° in the opposite direction.
Set them equal: qB = 2.0×(6/4)×(cos60°/cos45°) ≈ 2.1 nC. Both vertical components are upward.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Double the distance
steps: A point-charge field obeys E ∝ 1/r².
The outer radius is twice the inner radius.
The outer field is E/2² = E/4.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Symmetry points toward a negative vertex
steps: In B the two upper +q charges have horizontal components that cancel at P.
Their vertical components both point downward.
The lower −q also contributes downward, so the net field points directly toward the lower charge.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Mass and inverse-square scaling
steps: At twice the distance, electric force magnitude is one fourth as large.
Electron and proton have equal charge magnitude, but mp/me ≈ 1833.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: The nearest gap point wins
steps: Set the −3Q position to x = 0 and the +4Q position to x = 6a.
In units kQ/a², A has
B is largest: between the charges both fields point left and add.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Induced shell charges and field lines
steps: The negative inner sphere induces +Q on the shell’s inner face.
A neutral shell then has −Q on its outer face.
Field points inward in the gap and inward outside the shell, with no lines inside either conductor: option E.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: What the field tells you
steps: By definition E = F/q for a positive test charge.
Thus E gives force per unit charge and, once the test-charge sign is known, the force direction.
It does not tell you whether a charge actually occupies that location, so only I and II follow.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Graph the field magnitude
steps: At each point charge x = 2 and x = 4, the ideal point-charge field diverges.
Between equal positive charges the fields cancel at the midpoint x = 3.
A magnitude graph is nonnegative, has both divergences, and falls to zero at x = 3: option A.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Constant electric acceleration
steps: A uniform electric field produces constant force F = qE.
Therefore a = qE/m is constant.
For an electron q < 0, so the acceleration is opposite the field.
pitfall: Constant acceleration does not imply constant speed.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Zero closer to the smaller positive charge
steps: The fields oppose only between the two positive charges.
To balance +3q and +2q, the point must be farther from +3q and nearer +2q.
It lies between midpoint II and charge III.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Opposite unequal charges cancel outside
steps: Between −Q and +2Q both fields point left, so cancellation is impossible.
On the far right, the stronger and nearer +2Q always wins.
On the left of −Q, its shorter distance can compensate its smaller magnitude. Thus −∞ < x < 0.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Solve the external zero
steps: The zero is right of the smaller charge B, so x > 7 cm.
Set 3/(x−3)² = 2/(x−7)²; take positive square roots using the positive distances.
pitfall: The answer is a coordinate, not the distance measured from either charge.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Read arrow length in a vector plot
steps: This diagram uses separate arrows to represent field vectors.
Longer arrows mean greater field magnitude; the left column arrows are longest.
D is in the left column, so it has the strongest field.
pitfall: For a vector-arrow plot use arrow length; for continuous field lines use line density.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cavity, gap, and metal
steps: R is in an empty central cavity, so ER = 0; U is inside conducting material, so EU = 0.
S and T lie in the gap, where the enclosed charge is +10 nC and E = kq/r².
S is nearer the center than T, so ES > ET > ER = EU.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Field ratio is inverse-square
steps: EA = kq/r².
EB = kq/(2r)² = EA/4.
Therefore EA/EB = 4, not 1; equal flux does not mean equal field.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Compare spherical surface fields
steps: For each isolated sphere use E = kQ/R².
Divide: E1/E2 = (kQ1/R1²)/(kQ2/R2²).
Cancel k to obtain Q1R2²/(Q2R1²), option C.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Find a zero between positive spheres
steps: Let the position x lie between 0 and 0.20 m.
Set 2/x² = 6/(0.20−x)², since the fields oppose.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Distance ratio determines charge ratio
steps: P is d/4 to the right of +Q2, hence 5d/4 from −Q1.
The fields oppose; require Q1/(5d/4)² = Q2/(d/4)².
Thus Q1/Q2 = 5² = 25.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Integrate a nonuniform flux
steps: Use narrow vertical strips of area dA = b dx, because E varies with x.
Φ0 = ∫₀ᵃ Cx² b dx = Cba³/3.
Doubling a gives 8Φ0 (change 7Φ0); shifting to a…2a gives 7Φ0 (change 6Φ0); doubling b or C gives 2Φ0. B is largest.
pitfall: Compare changes, not merely the final expressions.
integration: Φ = ∫ E·dA. Here the field is normal, so Φ = Cb[x³/3]₀ᵃ. The cubic dependence is why length matters most.

title: Flux through faces at a charge corner
steps: Face P lies in a plane through the charge center, so the radial field is tangent to that face and its normal flux is zero.
Faces Q and R are equivalent by cube symmetry and each receives nonzero flux.
Therefore ΦQ = ΦR > ΦP.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Normal uniform flux
steps: Flux is Φ = EA cosθ, with θ measured from the normal.
Here θ = 0, so Φ = EA.
Solve for E = Φ/A.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A face in the source plane
steps: The charged sphere’s center lies in bottom face ABCD.
The radial field is tangent to that plane, so ΦABCD = 0.
The top face EFGH receives nonzero normal field; hence ΦEFGH > ΦABCD = 0.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Only the normal component counts
steps: Both surfaces lie in the xy plane, so only Ez contributes to flux.
The square has Φ = E0d².
The triangle has area d²/2 and Ez = 2E0, so it also has Φ = E0d².
pitfall: The x-components do not cross either surface.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cancel opposite faces first
steps: The constant x-component a gives equal outward and inward flux on opposite faces, canceling exactly.
For a cube of side L, Ez = bz e^(−cz) is zero at the bottom z = 0 and equals bL e^(−cL) at the top.
Net flux is bL³e^(−cL), which decreases as c increases.
pitfall: A uniform component may create flux through individual faces but zero net closed-surface flux.
integration: Evaluate ∮E·dA face by face; alternatively integrate divergence ∂Ez/∂z = b e^(−cz)(1−cz) over the cube.

title: A linearly varying field
steps: On the x = 0 face, Ex = 0.
On x = a, Ex = ba and area is a²; the other four faces have E·n = 0.
Net flux = ba×a² = ba³.
pitfall: Do not multiply one-face flux by six.
integration: ∮E·dA = ∫∫ba dy dz = ba³; equivalently ∇·E = b and ∫b dV = ba³.

title: Use concentric annuli
steps: Since x²+y² = r², the field is E = βr².
A thin circular annulus has area dA = 2πr dr.
Φ = ∫₀ᴿ βr²(2πr dr) = βπR⁴/2 = 100π(0.5)⁴/2 ≈ 9.8 N·m²/C.
pitfall: The field at the rim is not the field over the whole disk.
integration: The extra factor r comes from annular area: integrate r³, not r².

title: Projected area shortcut
steps: The electric field points along x, so Φ = E0Ax.
The triangle projects onto the yz plane as a right triangle with legs d and d.
Ax = d²/2, giving Φ = E0d²/2.
pitfall: Use the area component perpendicular to the field, not the full sloped area.
integration: A = √3 d²/2 and Ax = A/√3; integrating uniform E·n over the surface gives the same result.

title: Recover the field gradient
steps: A vertical strip has area dA = (0.50 m)dx.
Φ = ∫₀⁰·⁵ bx(0.50)dx = b/16 in SI units.
Setting Φ = 3.0 gives b = 48 N/(C·m).
pitfall: Using the field at x = 0.50 everywhere overestimates flux by a factor of two.

title: Compare solid angles
steps: X lies in Face A’s plane, so its field is tangent and ΦX = 0.
A centered charge Z sends one sixth of its total flux through Face A.
Y lies at the bottom center; Face A subtends a smaller solid angle than seen from Z, so 0 < ΦY < ΦZ. Thus D.
pitfall: Flux through an open face depends on geometry, unlike total flux through a closed surface.
integration: For a point-like sphere, Φface = qΩ/(4πε0); the center gives Ω = 2π/3, while the bottom-face center gives a smaller Ω.

title: Respect shifted integration limits
steps: The rectangle spans x0 to 3x0 and y0 to 2y0, so its strip height is y0.
Φ = y0∫x0^3x0 (a+bx) dx.
This is y0[2ax0+4bx0²] = 2x0y0(a+2bx0).
pitfall: The lower x limit is x0, not zero.
integration: Antiderivative: ax + bx²/2. Evaluate upper minus lower before simplifying.

title: Flux is independent of sphere radius
steps: Gauss’s law gives Φ = q/ε0 for every sphere enclosing the same charge.
The field decreases as 1/r² while area increases as r².
The graph is a positive horizontal line, A.
pitfall: This is flux versus radius, not electric field versus radius.
integration: ∮E·dA = [kq/r²](4πr²) = q/ε0.

title: Match the graph’s curvature
steps: For fixed orientation, Φ = Es² cosθN.
Flux grows quadratically with side length s, giving the upward-curving graph shown.
It is linear in E, decreases with θN over 0–90°, and is concave down in θP over that interval.
pitfall: Area is s², not s.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Use the face normal
steps: The right shaded face has outward normal +x.
Its area is (0.1 m)² = 0.01 m², and Ex = −100 N/C.
Signed flux is −1.0 N·m²/C, so its magnitude is 1.0: C.
pitfall: The y and z field components are parallel to this face.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Rotate through zero flux
steps: Initially the loop’s normal is parallel or antiparallel to E, giving maximum
Φ
= EA.
After 90° of rotation, its normal is perpendicular to E and Φ = 0.
After 180°,
Φ
returns to EA: decreases then increases.
pitfall: The signed flux reverses sign, but the question asks its magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Locate the negative flux maximum
steps: At bottom point P, the negative sphere pulls the field downward through the square.
The chosen area vector points upward, so flux is negative there and has maximum magnitude.
The graph’s negative minimum occurs at 3T/4.
pitfall: Field points toward a negative charge; use the signed normal component.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Angle from the plane
steps: The given 30° is measured from the plane, so the angle from the normal is 60°.
Φ = EA cos60° = EA/2.
Thus E = 2Φ/A.
pitfall: Do not put 30° directly into the cosine when the angle is to the plane.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Flux through annular strips
steps: At radius r, use dA = 2πr dr.
dΦ = [3(r+a)/π](2πr dr) = 6(r²+ar)dr.
Integrating from 0 to R gives Φ = 2R³+3aR².
pitfall: Do not use dA = dr or replace the nonuniform field by its rim value.
integration: Φ = 6∫₀ᴿ(r²+ar)dr = 6[r³/3+ar²/2]₀ᴿ.

title: Enclose only part of a sphere
steps: A radius-r Gaussian sphere has area 4πr².
Uniform charge density means Qenc/Q = r³/R³.
Gauss’s law gives E4πr² = (Q/ε0)(r³/R³), option D.
pitfall: Use the Gaussian radius r in the area, and the fraction of charge enclosed.
integration: Qenc = ∫₀ʳ [3Q/(4πR³)]4πs² ds = Qr³/R³.

title: Field inside and outside a cylinder
steps: Inside, enclosed charge per unit length grows as r², while Gaussian area per unit length grows as r.
Thus Ein ∝ r, beginning at zero at the axis.
Outside all the charge is enclosed, so Eout ∝ 1/r. The continuous rise-then-decay graph is A.
pitfall: A nonconducting charged volume does not have zero interior field.
integration: Qenc = ∫₀ʳρ2πsL ds; E2πrL = Qenc/ε0 gives E = ρr/(2ε0).

title: Uniform inner sphere with an outer shell
steps: For r < R, only the fraction r³/R³ of the insulating sphere’s charge is enclosed.
The external concentric shell does not alter this spherically symmetric interior field.
Gauss’s law is E4πr² = Qr³/(ε0R³), D.
pitfall: Do not include charges outside the Gaussian surface in Qenc.
integration: Integrate uniform density over the radius-r volume to get Qr³/R³.

title: Outside a neutral shell
steps: For r > b, the Gaussian sphere contains the inner charge Q and the shell’s zero net charge.
The enclosed net charge is Q.
Therefore E4πr² = Q/ε0, option B.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Density grows with radius
steps: A thin spherical shell has volume dV = 4πr²dr.
With ρ = βr, Qenc(r) = ∫₀ʳ 4πβs³ds = πβr⁴.
Flux is proportional to Qenc, so Φ(R)/Φ(R/2) = 2⁴ = 16.
pitfall: Density is not constant; using a volume ratio alone would give the wrong factor 8.
integration: Introduce s as the integration variable so the upper limit r is not confused with the variable inside the integral.

title: Induced charge from a varying density
steps: The insulating sphere’s charge is Q = ∫₀⁰·¹ βr³(4πr²dr).
The conductor must have −Q on its inner surface to make the field zero within its metal: approximately −13 μC.
pitfall: Grounding affects the outer-surface charge but does not remove the required inner-surface charge.
integration: The integrand is 4πβr⁵, so integrate to 4πβR⁶/6.

title: Long line fields fall as one over r
steps: Cylindrical Gauss’s law gives E = λ/(2πε0r).
Therefore E(5r0)/E(r0) = r0/(5r0).
The answer is E0/5.
pitfall: Inverse-square behavior is for a point charge, not an infinitely long line.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Superpose two positive sheets
steps: Each large sheet produces a nearly constant field σ/(2ε0), directed away from itself.
Between the sheets, the two contributions cancel, so EA = EB = 0.
Outside, the contributions add and are nearly distance-independent: EC = ED = EE > EA = EB.
pitfall: The approximation depends on distances being small compared with the sheet dimensions.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A radially increasing density
steps: Qenc(r) = ∫₀ʳ bs(4πs² ds) = πbr⁴.
E4πr² = Qenc/ε0 gives E(r) = br²/(4ε0).
At r = R/2, E = bR²/(16ε0).
pitfall: Do not multiply local density at r by the whole enclosed volume.
integration: The r³ integrand comes from density proportional to r times shell volume proportional to r²dr.

title: An approximately infinite sheet
steps: For a sheet much wider than the observation distances, E ≈ σ/(2ε0).
This expression is independent of perpendicular distance.
Thus the field at 2d is approximately E, not E/4.
pitfall: A finite sheet eventually has distance dependence; the stated a ≫ d approximation is essential.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Reduce line field by four
steps: For a very long line, E ∝ 1/r.
To make the field one quarter as large, the distance must be four times as large.
The required radius is 4r1.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Reduce line field by ten
steps: For a very long line, E = λ/(2πε0r).
Set Enew/E1 = r1/rnew = 1/10.
Therefore rnew = 10r1.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Count every enclosed signed charge
steps: The Gaussian radius is 0.80 m.
The figure places +3q at 0.60 m, −4q at the origin, and +2q at 0.30 m; all are inside.
Qenc = 3q−4q+2q = q, so Φ = q/ε0.
pitfall: Add signed charges, not their magnitudes.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: External charge gives zero net flux
steps: The source charge lies outside the closed cylinder.
The enclosed net charge is zero, so Gauss’s law gives Φnet = 0.
The field is not zero: as much flux enters as leaves.
pitfall: Zero net flux does not mean zero field or zero flux through each face.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Equal enclosed charge, equal flux
steps: Both spherical surfaces enclose the same +q.
Gauss’s law gives q/ε0 for each.
Therefore the outer flux is Φ, even though the outer field is smaller.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Integrate cylindrical shells
steps: A cylindrical shell of radius r and length L has volume dV = 2πrL dr.
With ρ = cr², Q(<r) = ∫₀ʳ 2πcLs³ds = (πcL/2)r⁴.
The fraction inside R/2 is (R/2)⁴/R⁴ = 1/16.
pitfall: For a cylinder the shell factor is r, not r².
integration: Density times shell volume produces r³dr; its integral scales as r⁴.

title: Fixed volume density at the surface
steps: For a uniform sphere, Q = 4πρ0R³/3.
The surface field is E = Q/(4πε0R²) = ρ0R/(3ε0).
Doubling R doubles E, so E2R = 2ER.
pitfall: Same density does not mean same total charge.
integration: Integrate ρ0 over spherical shells, then divide by Gaussian area.

title: What zero net flux requires
steps: Gauss’s law gives Φnet = Qenc/ε0.
If Φnet = 0, only Qenc = 0 is required.
Opposite charges may be enclosed, and external charges may produce a nonzero field. Thus only statement II must hold.
pitfall: The word must asks for a necessary statement, not one that is merely possible.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Share flux by symmetry
steps: The total flux from the centered charge is q/ε0.
A regular tetrahedron has four equivalent faces as viewed from its center.
Each face receives one fourth: q/(4ε0).
pitfall: Equal division requires the charge at the symmetry center.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A centered charge in a cube
steps: The diagram places +Q at the cube’s center.
Total flux is Q/ε0, and symmetry gives equal flux through all six faces.
Each face therefore has Q/(6ε0).
pitfall: The centered placement shown in the figure is needed; an arbitrary interior position would not give equal face fluxes.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Possible zero-flux situations
steps: An empty surface with no charges anywhere has zero enclosed charge and zero field.
This example satisfies I, II, and III simultaneously.
Thus all three could be true, even though only II must be true in every zero-flux situation.
pitfall: Distinguish could from must.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Flux enclosing one negative plate
steps: Only the −Q plate is inside the Gaussian surface.
Gauss’s law depends on enclosed signed charge, regardless of the other plate’s external field.
Thus Φ = −Q/ε0.
pitfall: Flux is not electric field: there is no extra area A in the denominator.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Field inside a uniformly charged sphere
steps: For r < R, E = kQr/R³.
Convert to SI: Q = 40×10⁻⁹ C, r = 0.020 m, R = 0.10 m.
pitfall: Using kQ/r² incorrectly puts the full sphere charge inside the small Gaussian surface.
integration: Qenc = Q(r/R)³; substituting into E = kQenc/r² yields kQr/R³.

title: Ignore external charge in net flux
steps: The cube encloses +3.0 nC; the −3.0 nC charge is outside.
Net flux is Qenc/ε0 = 3.0×10⁻⁹/(8.85×10⁻¹²).
The magnitude is about 339 ≈ 340 N·m²/C.
pitfall: The exterior charge changes how flux is distributed among faces but not the total.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Use two radial laws
steps: Inside the sphere, E(r) = ER(r/R), so E(R/3) = ER/3.
Outside, E(r) = ER(R/r)², so E(3R) = ER/9.
Thus ER > ER/3 > E3R.
pitfall: The interior field is linear, while the exterior field is inverse-square.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Closed-surface shape does not matter
steps: Both surfaces enclose exactly the same charge +Q.
Gauss’s law gives Q/ε0 for each closed-surface flux.
Equal area is irrelevant; equal enclosed charge is the correct reason.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Cylinder around a charged line
steps: Use a coaxial Gaussian cylinder: only its curved side has flux.
E(2πrL) = λL/ε0, so E = λ/(2πε0r).
With λ = 4.0×10⁻⁹ C/m and r = 0.20 m, E ≈ 360 N/C.
pitfall: The Gaussian length L cancels; it is not a physical dependence.
integration: Direct Coulomb integration gives E = kλ∫₋∞^∞ r dz/(r²+z²)^(3/2) = 2kλ/r, identical to Gauss’s law.

title: Integrate only charged material
steps: The hollow region r < ra contains no charge.
For a Gaussian radius r in the tube, Qenc = ∫raʳ βs³(2πsL ds) = (2πβL/5)(r⁵−ra⁵).
Divide by ε0(2πrL): E = β(r⁵−ra⁵)/(5ε0r).
pitfall: The lower integration limit is ra, and the upper limit is the observation radius r, not rb.
integration: A cylindrical shell contributes dQ = ρ(s)2πsL ds; keep the dummy radius s separate from the outer radius r.

title: Superpose a central charge and a volume charge
steps: At r = RS/2, the uniform sphere contributes Qenc = Q(1/2)³ = Q/8.
The central particle contributes its full charge q to the same Gaussian surface.
Both are positive, so E = [q+Q/8]/[4πε0(RS/2)²].
pitfall: A central point charge and distributed sphere may share one Gaussian calculation because the arrangement remains spherical.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: A pillbox has two active faces
steps: The infinite sheet’s field is normal to the sheet and equal on both sides.
The two flat caps each contribute EA; the curved side contributes zero.
Enclosed charge is σA, so 2EA = σA/ε0.
pitfall: Do not count only one cap unless the other lies in a conductor where E = 0.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: An increasing slab density
steps: Use the intended reference E0 at the slab surfaces z = ±z0 (the statement’s subscript is faint/ambiguous).
For a symmetric pillbox extending to ±z, Qenc = 2A∫₀ᶻ Cs ds = ACz².
2EA = ACz²/ε0 gives E ∝ z²; at z0/2 the field is E0/4.
pitfall: The printed reference uses ±z rather than clearly ±z0; the answer choices assume the boundary value.
integration: Integrate the varying density through the slab before applying Gauss’s law: E(z) = Cz²/(2ε0) for 0 ≤ z ≤ z0.

title: Interior of a uniform solid cylinder
steps: The total linear density is λ, so volume density is ρ = λ/(πR²).
Inside radius r, Qenc = ρπr²L = λLr²/R².
E2πrL = Qenc/ε0 gives E = λr/(2πε0R²).
pitfall: Use the enclosed area fraction r²/R², not the volume fraction for a sphere.
integration: Qenc = ∫₀ʳρ2πsL ds = ρπr²L.

title: Integrate a spherical density
steps: Use dQ = βs(4πs²ds).
Qenc(r) = πβr⁴ and E(r) = Qenc/(4πε0r²) = βr²/(4ε0).
At r = R/2, E = βR²/(16ε0).
pitfall: ρ(r) is a local density, not the average density inside r.
integration: ∫₀ʳ4πβs³ds = πβr⁴; the fourth power in Q becomes the second power in E.

title: Flux ratio for concentric spheres
steps: Each Gaussian surface encloses the same +q.
Thus ΦA = q/ε0 = ΦB.
Their ratio is 1; the larger area exactly compensates the smaller field.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Where a sphere and shell look alike
steps: Outside radius R, both spherically symmetric objects have E = kQ/r² and V = kQ/r with zero at infinity.
Points C, D, and E all lie outside the sphere.
Inside, a conductor shell has E = 0 and constant V, while a uniformly charged solid sphere has varying E and V. Therefore only C, D, E match.
pitfall: At the center both fields are zero, but their potentials differ, so A does not satisfy both conditions.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Move an external charge
steps: Moving Y outside the cube does not change the charge enclosed around X.
Gauss’s law therefore keeps the total flux fixed.
Y does change the local field pattern and the flux through individual faces: option E.
pitfall: The source figure labels Y with −4Φ0, not −Φ0/4; extraction can reverse that notation.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Conserve charge before sharing
steps: Initial charges are QX = ε0Φ0 and QY = −4ε0Φ0.
The total is −3ε0Φ0; identical touching conductors share it equally when separated far apart.
Each ends at −3ε0Φ0/2, so the flux around X is −3Φ0/2.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Enclose both conductors
steps: Contact redistributes charge but cannot change the pair’s total.
The initial total charge corresponds to flux Φ0−4Φ0 = −3Φ0.
With both conductors inside the Gaussian cube, the net flux is −3Φ0 regardless of their separation.
pitfall: Keep the direction and sign separate from the magnitude.
integration: This is a discrete-charge or conceptual problem; integration adds no simplification. Use the stated conservation, symmetry, or superposition argument.

title: Opposite charges have negative energy
steps: Choose U=0 at infinite separation.
U(r)=k(+Q)(−Q)/r=−kQ²/r. It is negative, rises toward zero as r increases, and becomes more negative as the charges approach.
Graph B has this shape.
pitfall: A negative U can increase: −1 J is higher than −5 J.
integration: U(r)=−∫∞ʳ F_r ds=−∫∞ʳ (−kQ²/s²)ds=−kQ²/r.

title: Count the three distinct pairs
steps: For either triangle, the pair products are +Q², −Q², and −Q².
All three separations are s, so each total is −kQ²/s.
The sign of a charge matters, but the collection of pair products is the same here.
pitfall: The potential at the center is not the total energy of the three-charge arrangement.
integration: Assemble charges one at a time. Each new charge contributes qV_existing, obtained by integrating the resisting external force from infinity.

title: Add a charge without changing total energy
steps: The original two-charge energy stays fixed. The added energy is kq(2Q/r₊−Q/r₋).
Set the added energy to zero: 2/r₊=1/r₋, hence r₊=2r₋.
The new charge must be closer to the smaller-magnitude source, −Q. This is the controlling reason in C.
pitfall: Opposite sign alone does not determine the required distance ratio.
integration: ΔU=−q∫∞ᴾ E_existing·dl=qV_existing(P); require this integral to vanish.

title: Rank signed pair energies
steps: Compare q₁q₂/r in common nC²/cm units.
The four values are 1, 1, −6, and 2.
Therefore U₄>U₁=U₂>U₃.
pitfall: Rank signed energies, not their absolute magnitudes.
integration: Integrating the radial Coulomb force gives kq₁q₂/r, so inverse distance rather than inverse distance squared controls U.

title: Sum pair energies in three geometries
steps: Use kQ²/s as a common unit. X gives 2+2+1=5.
Y has three pairs of 2Q charges, giving 4+4+4=12.
Z gives √2+1+1=2+√2. Thus UY>UX>UZ.
pitfall: Include the long end-to-end pair in the straight-line arrangement.
integration: For each added charge integrate −qE_existing·dl from infinity; linearity makes the result the sum of all distinct kqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ terms.

title: Adding a negative charge lowers energy
steps: The two positive charges retain their original positive pair energy.
Adding −Q₃ adds two negative pair energies, −kQ₁Q₃/r₁₃−kQ₂Q₃/r₂₃.
Thus UY<UX; a slow external placement requires negative work, while the electric field does positive work.
pitfall: Attraction means the field helps the motion; the external force removes energy.
integration: W_ext=−∫F_electric·dl=ΔU<0 for quasistatic insertion.

title: Energy is a pairwise sum
steps: Every distinct pair contributes kQ²/rᵢⱼ.
Add each pair exactly once: U₀=Σᵢ<ⱼ kQ²/rᵢⱼ.
There is no additional separate three-charge term in this electrostatic point-charge model.
pitfall: Summing over all ordered i,j pairs counts each interaction twice.
integration: Integrate the work of adding charges successively; each added charge interacts with all earlier charges once.

title: Track one pair rather than the whole system
steps: For the negative source and the incoming positive charge, U₋₃=−kQ₀Q₃/r.
As their distance decreases from very large to 2D, this energy becomes more negative.
Therefore that pair's energy becomes lower, even though the total added energy from both sources is positive.
pitfall: Do not substitute the total system's energy for the specific pair named in the option.
integration: ΔU₋₃=−∫∞²ᴰ (−kQ₀Q₃/r²)dr=−kQ₀Q₃/(2D).

title: Compare line and triangle
steps: In units kQ²/s, system A has −2−2+1/2=−3.5.
System B has −2−2+1=−3.
Because −3>−3.5, UB>UA.
pitfall: A larger-magnitude negative number is a lower energy.
integration: Only the positive-positive pair changes separation; its integrated assembly work rises from kQ²/(2s) to kQ²/s.

title: Energy and field work have opposite signs
steps: At the final upper-right corner the added +q is a side length a from +q and a diagonal √2a from −q.
ΔU=kq²/a−kq²/(√2a)>0.
The electric force does W_electric=−ΔU<0. Choose positive ΔU and negative electric work.
pitfall: Use distances to both existing charges, including the diagonal.
integration: W_electric=q∫∞ᴾ E·dl=−q[V(P)−V(∞)].

title: Electrostatic work is path independent
steps: Both paths have identical initial and final separations.
ΔU=kq₁q₂(1/r_f−1/r_i) is the same for both and is positive.
For the intended comparison with the same kinetic-energy change (in particular slow motion), W_ext=ΔU is also the same.
pitfall: If an external agent also changed final kinetic energy, its total work would include ΔK; the electrostatic contribution remains path independent.
integration: The line integral of an electrostatic field depends only on endpoints: ∮E·dl=0.

title: Assembling the third equal charge
steps: Let each charge be q. Bringing particle 2 to D costs W₂=kq²/D.
Particle 3 is distance D from particle 2 and 2D from particle 1, so W₃=kq²/D+kq²/(2D)=1.5W₂.
Both earlier particles repel the incoming one.
pitfall: The third charge interacts with both existing charges, not only its nearest neighbor.
integration: Integrate the sum of the two repulsive forces; integration is linear, giving the sum of their two potential-energy terms.

title: Assembly energy depends on final configuration
steps: All three procedures start with the pair infinitely separated and end with separation 1 cm.
The final energy is k(1 nC)(2 nC)/(1 cm), irrespective of which charge moved.
For equal endpoint kinetic energies the total external work is the same in all three procedures.
pitfall: Moving both charges does not double the pair energy.
integration: Total work ∫(F₁·dr₁+F₂·dr₂) reduces to the integral over the relative separation, yielding the same ΔU.

title: Use distances from the requested point
steps: The diagram places +3 μC at x=3 cm and −2 μC at x=7 cm. At x=6 cm the distances are 0.03 m and 0.01 m.
This is −9.0×10⁵ V.
pitfall: Use distance from each source, not each source's coordinate.
integration: Integrate each radial field from infinity, then add the signed potentials kq/r.

title: Four charges have six pairs
steps: For four charges the number of distinct pairs is 4×3/2=6.
Every edge of the regular tetrahedron is L, so every pair contributes kQ²/L.
U=6kQ²/L=6Q²/(4πε₀L).
pitfall: Four charges do not mean four interacting pairs.
integration: Sequential assembly produces 0+1+2+3 pair contributions, each equal to the Coulomb-force work integral kQ²/L.

title: Positive and negative energies
steps: In units kQ²/r, the arrangements have energies A=1, B=1/2, C=−1, D=−1/2.
Positive energies exceed negative energies.
The order is UA>UB>UD>UC.
pitfall: For unlike charges, increasing separation makes U less negative and therefore higher.
integration: U=−∫∞ʳ F_r ds preserves the sign of the pair product.

title: Potential energy scales as inverse separation
steps: Two negative charges have a positive product q₁q₂.
U=kq₁q₂/x; replacing x with 3x gives U_new=U/3.
The sign stays positive.
pitfall: The inverse-square law is for force; energy varies as 1/r.
integration: Integrating a 1/r² force over distance produces a 1/r energy.

title: Proton–electron–proton assembly
steps: There are two attractive proton-electron pairs at distance a, each with energy −ke²/a.
The proton-proton pair is repulsive and separated by 2a, contributing +ke²/(2a).
Total external assembly work is −3ke²/(2a).
pitfall: Do not omit the proton-proton repulsion.
integration: Sum the three quasistatic work integrals; each is kqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ.

title: Express all pairs in the given energy unit
steps: The diagram gives q₁=+q, q₂=−q, q₃=−q at x=0,2d,3d. The q₂–q₃ energy is U=kq²/d.
The other two terms are −U/2 and −U/3.
U_total=U−U/2−U/3=U/6.
pitfall: The q₁–q₂ separation is 2d, not d.
integration: Assembly work equals the sum of the Coulomb-force integrals for the three distinct separations.

title: Bring two charges together from rest
steps: Initial U and K are zero; final K is zero.
The final pair energy is +kq₁q₂/d.
The external force supplies this energy, so W_ext=+kq₁q₂/d.
pitfall: Electric work is the negative of external work in this rest-to-rest assembly.
integration: W_ext=−∫∞ᵈ kq₁q₂/r² dr=+kq₁q₂/d.

title: Numerical triangle assembly energy
steps: The three charges are +2, −4, and −2 μC; all separations are 0.15 m.
Their pair products sum to −8−4+8=−4 μC².
pitfall: Microcoulomb squared means 10⁻¹² C².
integration: Assemble sequentially and integrate the external force; the resulting pair energies include both attractions and repulsion.

title: Three signed pair products
steps: The charges are −2q, +2q, +3q at equal separation s.
The pair products are −4q², −6q², +6q².
W_ext=U_final=−4kq²/s.
pitfall: Adding charge values first and squaring would include unphysical self-energy terms.
integration: The three pairwise assembly integrals add to k[−4−6+6]q²/s.

title: Cancel scalar potentials at a square's center
steps: All four corners are the same distance from the center, so V=kΣq/r.
The three given charges already sum to +10+10−20=0 μC.
The fourth charge must be zero.
pitfall: Potential is a signed scalar sum; do not add field vectors here.
integration: V=∫k dq/r; for discrete charges at one common distance this becomes kΣq/r.

title: Separate plates at fixed charge
steps: For large plates of fixed area, fixed charge means fixed σ and E=σ/ε₀.
The magnitude of their voltage difference is Ed.
Increasing d therefore increases the voltage difference while E remains constant.
pitfall: This is fixed charge, not a battery maintaining fixed voltage.
integration: |ΔV|=|−∫E·dl|=Ed because E is uniform along the perpendicular path.

title: Kinetic energy from the same voltage
steps: The electric energy gain through a given accelerating voltage magnitude is
q
V.
Lithium receives 3qV; helium receives 2qV.
The energy-gain ratio is 3/2, independent of their masses.
pitfall: Mass affects speed, not the work done by a specified potential difference.
integration: W=q∫E·dl=−qΔV; compare the charges when ΔV is the same.

title: Stopping in a stronger reversed field
steps: In region I the particle gains kinetic energy
q
E₀d.
In region II the force opposes its motion; stopping after distance x removes
q
(3E₀)x.
Equate the gained and lost energy to find x=d/3.
pitfall: The full width 2d is not the stopping distance.
integration: The total work ∫qE_x dx over both regions is zero: |q|E₀d−3|q|E₀x=0.

title: Solve for the second zero-potential point
steps: The diagram places −2Q at x=D and +Q at x=2D.
Between the charges, V=0 requires −2/(x−D)+1/(2D−x)=0.
Thus x−D=2(2D−x), giving x=5D/3.
pitfall: Distances are positive; use different distance expressions in different coordinate intervals.
integration: Integrating each source field gives kq/r; zero total potential requires cancellation of these signed integrals.

title: Move along an equipotential
steps: No field work at any moment means qE·dl=0 throughout the motion.
Therefore each displacement is perpendicular to E and tangent to an equipotential.
The charge moves along an equipotential line.
pitfall: Perpendicular to an equipotential is along the field, generally doing work.
integration: dV=−E·dl=0 at each step; integrating gives unchanged V.

title: Positive external work on a positive charge
steps: Read the map: A and C are +2 V, B is +6 V, and D is −6 V.
For rest-to-rest motion W_ext=q(V_f−V_i).
Only D→B raises the potential among the listed choices, so it requires positive work.
pitfall: Work depends on voltage change, not how long the route is.

title: Equal potential means zero field work
steps: A and C both lie on the +2 V contour.
Their potential difference is zero, so W_field=−qΔV=0 for any charge sign.
Therefore choose A and C.
pitfall: A negative charge changes the work sign but cannot change zero into nonzero.
integration: The line integral between points on the same electrostatic equipotential is zero even along a curved route.

title: Identify opposite charge sources
steps: The upper contours surround a positive-potential source and the lower contours a negative one.
The pattern has opposite signs on opposite sides and a zero line between.
Of the choices, two long lines with opposite charge signs can produce this cross section.
pitfall: Two negative point charges cannot create the shown positive-potential region when V(∞)=0.
integration: For an infinite line, potential differences vary as −(λ/2πε₀)ln(r_f/r_i); opposite line charges superpose into the shown opposite-sign pattern.

title: Electron speed versus voltage
steps: From rest, (1/2)mv²=e
V
Solving gives v=√(2e
V
Thus speed is proportional to √V for the positive voltage magnitude used in the question.
pitfall: Speed does not grow linearly with voltage.
integration: ∫mv dv=e∫d|V| yields the square-root dependence.

title: Bring a positive charge toward two positive sources
steps: If the triangle side is a, VI=2kQ/a and VII=4kQ/a.
Moving +q from I to II increases U by q(VII−VI)>0.
Constant speed means ΔK=0, so W_ext>0 and W_electric<0.
pitfall: At II the net field can be zero while the potential is large.
integration: The electric work integral equals −q(VII−VI); the external integral has the opposite sign for constant speed.

title: Compare potentials at two symmetric points
steps: At I both source distances are a; at II both are a/2.
VI=2kQ/a and VII=2kQ/(a/2)=4kQ/a.
Hence VI<VII.
pitfall: Do not infer potential from net field cancellation at the midpoint.
integration: V=Σ∫k dq/r; every source is twice as close at II, so each scalar contribution doubles.

title: A negative charge accelerates toward a positive sheet
steps: The moving charge is −q, so U=−qV.
Conservation gives (1/2)mv²=q(VS−VT).
Therefore v=√[2q(VS−VT)/m].
pitfall: The q in the options is a positive magnitude; the particle's signed charge is −q.
integration: W=∫(−q)E·dl=q(VS−VT); use the voltage endpoints without assuming a constant field over the entire region.

title: Potential difference inside a uniform sphere
steps: Potential has units kQ/length, which immediately selects Q/(8πε₀a).
For a uniform volume charge, E(r)=kQr/a³ inside.
V_center−V_surface=∫₀ᵃ E(r)dr=kQ/(2a)=Q/(8πε₀a).
pitfall: The sphere is uniformly charged throughout its volume, not a conducting shell.
integration: The integral of r is r²/2; this produces the factor 1/2.

title: Closest contours mean strongest field
steps: The diagram uses equal 2 V increments between neighboring equipotentials.
Near A the same voltage change occurs over the shortest perpendicular distance.
Therefore
E
ΔV/Δs
is greatest at A; C and D are inside a constant-potential region.
pitfall: The largest value of V need not have the largest field.
integration: E is the local derivative −dV/ds, the inverse operation to ΔV=−∫E·dl.

title: Work along a multi-segment route
steps: Point A is at −1 V and point D is in the 7 V region.
The result is 16 μJ, independent of the intermediate B and C points.
pitfall: Use the endpoint potentials; the curved path does not add extra electrostatic work.
integration: The integrals over AB, BC, and CD add to −q∫Aᴰ E·dl=q(VD−VA).

title: Compare signed potentials near unequal charges
steps: Let adjacent grid spacing be ℓ. Set +4Q at x=0 and −3Q at x=5ℓ; A,B,C,D,E are x=−ℓ,ℓ,3ℓ,4ℓ,6ℓ.
In units kQ/ℓ their potentials are 4−3/6, 4−3/4, 4/3−3/2, 1−3, and 4/6−3.
A has the largest value, 3.5.
pitfall: Being close to a negative charge lowers the scalar potential.
integration: Each term is the integrated field of one source, kq/r; keep the negative source term signed.

title: Find the most crowded contours
steps: Each neighboring contour differs by 5 V.
The lines are closest together near B.
Thus the electric field magnitude is greatest there.
pitfall: Count voltage change per perpendicular distance, not the absolute voltage.
integration: The steepest spatial rate of change |dV/ds| gives the largest field.

title: Field points downhill in potential
steps: At A the contour tangent runs down and right; the field must be perpendicular to it.
The 0 V side is up and right from the 5 V contour.
E therefore points up-right, as vector A shows.
pitfall: The field points from higher potential to lower potential.
integration: For a small step along E, dV=−E ds<0.

title: External work on a negative charge
steps: C lies on 10 V and E on 20 V.
For a rest-to-rest transfer, W_ext=qΔV=(−1 μC)(20−10 V).
W_ext=−10 μJ: the field releases energy that the external agent removes.
pitfall: The minus sign of the test charge reverses the energy change.
integration: W_ext=−q∫Cᴱ E·dl=qΔV.

title: Scale the scalar charge sum
steps: Initially V=k(Q+2Q)/d=3kQ/d.
The new charges are 2Q and 6Q, so V_new=8kQ/d.
Therefore V_new=(8/3)V.
pitfall: Tripling Q₂=2Q makes it 6Q, not 3Q.
integration: At common distance d, the potential integral is proportional to the total charge.

title: Match battery voltage and polarity
steps: The right plate is at +2 V and the left at −2 V, so right minus left is +4 V.
Two 2 V cells must be in series aiding, with their net positive terminal connected to the right plate.
Configuration D gives that polarity and 4 V difference.
pitfall: A single 2 V cell cannot produce a 4 V plate difference.
integration: The electric field between the plates integrates to a 4 V difference; the battery series voltages add around the circuit.

title: Zero potential does not mean zero force
steps: Potential increases to the right, so E points left.
An electron has negative charge and therefore feels force to the right.
The magnitude requires E=
ΔV
/spacing, but no physical spacing is supplied.
pitfall: The arbitrary 0 V label does not make E or force vanish.
integration: E=−dV/dx; a nonzero slope remains at the point where V=0.

title: Read a field direction from contours
steps: At D the equipotential runs up-right, so the field must point across it.
Lower potentials lie up-left; higher potentials lie down-right.
The field is up-left, vector C.
pitfall: Do not point E along an equipotential line.
integration: A small displacement up-left gives dV<0; since dV=−E·dl, E points that way.

title: Compare spacing on a second map
steps: Adjacent contours differ by 1 V.
They are most tightly packed near A.
The same voltage change over the smallest distance means the largest field magnitude.
pitfall: A contour's numerical label alone says nothing about its local field strength.
integration: Compare |dV/ds| in the direction normal to each contour.

title: Work between points on one contour
steps: A and B lie on the same −2 V equipotential.
ΔV=0, so W_electric=−qΔV=0.
This remains true for the electron's negative charge.
pitfall: Electrostatic work depends only on endpoints, not path.
integration: ∫Bᴬ E·dl=0 because VA=VB.

title: Energy released along a charged ring's axis
steps: The ring-axis potential is V(x)=kQ/√(R²+x²).
At x=R it is kQ/(√2R); at x=2R it is kQ/(√5R).
pitfall: The distance to ring charge is √(R²+x²), not x.
integration: K=∫R²ᴿ q[kQx/(R²+x²)^(3/2)]dx; the antiderivative is −kQq/√(R²+x²).

title: Find where the potential slope vanishes
steps: E_x=−dV/dx=−R+2Sx.
This is 0.1875 m≈0.19 m.
pitfall: V=0 and E=0 are different equations.
integration: Differentiate the potential; integrating the resulting field back recovers V up to a constant.

title: Work on a proton between plates
steps: The proton moves 0.75 cm=0.0075 m along E.
Its gained kinetic energy is eEd=(1.60×10⁻¹⁹)(95)(0.0075).
pitfall: Convert centimeters to meters.
integration: K=e∫Aᴮ E_x dx=eE(xB−xA), since E is constant.

title: Parallel capacitors share voltage
steps: Each capacitor has 9 V across it.
E=V/d depends on separation, not plate area, under the ideal large-plate approximation.
I and III have separation d and equal fields; II has 2d and half their field.
pitfall: Area changes capacitance and charge at fixed V, but not E when d is fixed.
integration: The relation V=|∫E·dl|=Ed gives the field for each gap.

title: Field direction from labeled curves
steps: Potential rises from 10 V on the left to 40 V on the right.
Near P the curves are approximately vertical, so the field is approximately horizontal.
E points toward lower V: to the left.
pitfall: A positive potential does not imply a rightward field.
integration: E_x=−∂V/∂x; the positive x slope of V makes E_x negative.

title: Estimate the local field magnitude
steps: Near P the adjacent 20 V and 30 V contours are roughly 0.04 m apart.
The magnitude is approximately
ΔV
This is about 250 V/m.
pitfall: Use the difference between nearby contour values, not the absolute 25 V at P.
integration: The finite difference approximates the derivative magnitude |dV/dx|.

title: Differentiate with respect to the varying coordinate
steps: V depends only on y, so E_x=0 and E_y=−(8y−3).
At (2,6), insert y=6 to obtain E_y=−45 V/m.
The requested magnitude is 45 N/C.
pitfall: The x-coordinate 2 does not enter a potential that depends only on y.
integration: E_y=−dV/dy; integrating −E_y restores 4y²−3y plus a constant.

title: Take the negative derivative
steps: For V=−4x²+3x+8, dV/dx=−8x+3.
Therefore E_x=−dV/dx=8x−3.
The constant 8 contributes zero field.
pitfall: Do not forget the overall minus sign.
integration: ΔV=−∫E_x dx; differentiating is the inverse relationship.

title: Integrate through space and metal
steps: Below the positive sheet the field points downward; above it the field points upward. Its outside magnitude is 100 N/C, and E=0 inside the conducting slab.
Going upward from Y to X gives +1 V over the 1 cm below the sheet, −2 V over the gap, zero through the slab, and −1 V above it.
VX−VY=−2 V, so the magnitude is 2 V.
pitfall: The field reverses direction across the sheet; adding every distance with the same sign is wrong.
integration: Split ΔV=−∫E_y dy into four regions, using the correct sign of E_y and zero field in the conductor.

title: Signed potential of two point charges
steps: Distances to the origin are 0.20 m and 0.10 m.
The result is −180+450=270 V.
pitfall: Use signed source charges but positive distances.
integration: Superpose the two radial field integrals, each giving kq/r.

title: A positive slope gives a negative field
steps: V=kx² gives E_x=−2kx.
At x=3 m and k=3 V/m², E_x=−18 V/m.
The sign specifies the negative x-direction.
pitfall: The question asks for the signed field, not only its magnitude.
integration: E_x=−dV/dx follows from differentiating ΔV=−∫E_x dx.

title: Unequal corner charges at the center
steps: The charges sum to +2Q+2Q−Q−Q=2Q.
Each source is distance a/√2 from P.
V=k(2Q)/(a/√2)=Q/(√2πε₀a), option B.
pitfall: The center-to-corner distance is half the diagonal, not a.
integration: At common distance r the potential superposition integral factors as (k/r)∫dq.

title: Four identical corner charges
steps: Each corner is a/√2 from the center.
All four positive scalar contributions add: V=4kq/(a/√2).
Thus V=4√2kq/a.
pitfall: The electric field cancels at the center, but the potential does not.
integration: V=Σ∫k dq/r=4kq/r; there is no directional cancellation in this scalar integral.

title: Dipole potential on the perpendicular bisector
steps: P is the same distance a from +Q and −Q.
V(P)=kQ/a−kQ/a=0.
This does not mean the electric field is zero at P.
pitfall: Potential cancellation and vector-field cancellation are different.
integration: The two signed field integrals from infinity to P cancel in potential.

title: Energy of the two-charge configuration
steps: Only the actual +Q and −Q charges contribute to this pair energy; P is just a location.
Their separation is a.
U=k(+Q)(−Q)/a=−Q²/(4πε₀a).
pitfall: Do not treat the labeled point P as a third charge.
integration: Bring the second charge from infinity: W_ext=−∫∞ᵃ (−kQ²/r²)dr=−kQ²/a.

title: Potential between concentric shells
steps: For r₁<r<r₂, the inner shell contributes kQ₁/r.
The outer shell contributes the constant interior potential kQ₂/r₂.
Therefore V=k(Q₁/r+Q₂/r₂), proportional to the expression in E.
pitfall: An outer shell contributes no interior field but does contribute a nonzero constant potential.
integration: Integrate the field piecewise inward from infinity, or integrate each shell's potential contribution separately.

title: Only displacement parallel to the field counts
steps: E=6000 V/m points right; Y is 0.40 m to the right of X.
The question asks VX−VY, so the answer is +2400 V.
pitfall: The vertical 0.30 m and diagonal 0.50 m do not enter this horizontal field integral.
integration: −∫Xʸ E·dl=−∫ E dx; the y part has zero dot product.

title: Use radial distances in two dimensions
steps: This is about 1.46−2.85=−1.39 V, closest to −1.38 V.
pitfall: Coordinates are not distances from the source; use the Pythagorean theorem.
integration: The conservative line integral equals kQ(1/rB−1/rA), regardless of the route between A and B.

title: A straight potential graph
steps: The graph rises linearly with x, so dV/dx is a constant positive value.
E_x=−dV/dx is therefore constant and negative.
Choose C.
pitfall: The height of the graph is potential; its slope determines field.
integration: A constant field integrates to a linear potential.

title: Field from a curved potential graph
steps: The plotted V increases but becomes progressively flatter toward x=2 cm.
Thus dV/dx is positive and decreases to zero.
E_x is negative and rises toward zero, matching B.
pitfall: Do not copy the shape of V directly into the E graph.
integration: The change in V over an interval is the negative area under E; a shrinking negative E produces progressively smaller positive increments of V.

title: Numerical ring-axis potential
steps: First find total ring charge: Q=λ(2πR)=2.513 μC.
Every ring element is distance √(0.40²+0.20²)=0.4472 m from P.
V=kQ/r≈50.6 kV, positive on either side of the ring.
pitfall: A negative x-coordinate does not make the distance or the potential of a positive ring negative.
integration: V=∫₀²π kλR dθ/√(R²+x²)=2πkλR/√(R²+x²).

title: Zero field from a quadratic potential
steps: Differentiate V=ax−bx²: E_x=−a+2bx.
Set E_x=0.
The solution is x=a/(2b), assuming b≠0 as intended.
pitfall: Solving V=0 would instead find zeros of the potential.
integration: The field is the negative derivative of potential, not its integral.

title: Potential inside a cavity, in metal, and outside
steps: The metal is an equipotential. The positive charge in its cavity raises the potential at cavity point X above the metal value at Y.
The neutral conductor has induced +Q on its outer surface, so the outside potential decreases away from that surface to Z.
Therefore VZ<VY<VX.
pitfall: E=0 applies in the metal, not throughout the charged cavity.
integration: Along outward field lines from the positive cavity charge and from the outer surface, ΔV=−∫E·dl<0.

title: Add sphere and induced-surface potentials
steps: At the center, the uniform solid sphere contributes 3kQ/(2a).
The neutral metal shell acquires −Q at radius b and +Q at radius c; their interior potentials are −kQ/b and +kQ/c.
Total V=kQ(1.5/a−1/b+1/c).
pitfall: The shell's zero net charge does not mean its two surface contributions cancel at different radii.
integration: Equivalently integrate inward from infinity with E=kQ/r² outside c and between a,b, E=0 in metal, and E=kQr/a³ inside the sphere.

title: Two equal positive charges
steps: Both +4.0 μC charges are 2.0 m from the origin.
Their potentials add: V=2k(4.0×10⁻⁶)/2.0.
pitfall: Their fields cancel at the origin; their positive potentials add.
integration: Each source contributes the radial integral kq/r.

title: Set up the potential of a finite rod
steps: Choose x from the left end, so dq=λ₀dx and 0≤x≤L.
P is above the midpoint x=L/2. A source element at x is distance √[(x−L/2)²+D²] from P.
Therefore V=k∫₀ᴸ λ₀dx/√[(x−L/2)²+D²], option D.
