pitfall: The distance to each rod element varies; D alone is not the denominator.
integration: Use dV=k dq/r, substitute the charge element and geometry, and only then set limits.

title: Integrate around a ring
steps: Every ring element has the same distance √(R²+D²) from P.
Take that common denominator outside V=∫k dq/r.
The remaining ∫dq=Q gives V=kQ/√(R²+D²).
pitfall: The ring-axis field has an extra projection factor; the potential does not.
integration: One may write dq=λR dθ and integrate θ from 0 to 2π, obtaining k(2πRλ)/√(R²+D²).

title: Proton and electron energy gains
steps: Both particles cross the same voltage magnitude and both have charge magnitude e.
Each starts at rest, so K_f=e
ΔV
Their final kinetic energies are equal; their final speeds are not.
pitfall: The much lighter electron travels faster, but receives the same electric work.
integration: W=q∫E·dl has the same positive value for the two opposite charges moving in opposite directions.

title: A negative charge near a potential maximum
steps: Near N the contours have higher potential inward, reaching 6 V; a negative charge has U=qV, so this is a local low-U region in the shown plane.
Released nearby, the negative test charge is attracted toward the high-V region and remains nearby in the intended map interpretation.
Thus D is the supported choice; H has wider contours than J, L is a low-potential region, and E at M is not horizontal.
pitfall: This is the behavior inferred from the supplied planar map; a map alone does not establish stable three-dimensional trapping in charge-free electrostatics.
integration: F=−∇U=−q∇V; with q<0 it points toward increasing V.

title: Count contour intervals
steps: Between the 0 kV contour and the labeled ±5 kV contours are five equal 1 kV steps.
A lies on −3 kV; B lies on +5 kV.
The magnitude of the difference is
=8 kV.
pitfall: Count contour crossings carefully; B is on the innermost +5 kV curve.
integration: Potential differences are the negative field integral; the contour labels already encode this integral.

title: Potential along the bisector of two positive charges
steps: Along B→D, both source distances are equal at every point.
They decrease toward the midpoint of BD and then increase symmetrically, so V=2kQ/√(d²+y²) has a positive central maximum.
Graph C shows this symmetric positive hump.
pitfall: The field at the midpoint is zero, but V is largest there along this path.
integration: Integrating dV=k dq/r for the two charges gives the formula; differentiating it gives zero slope at the midpoint.

title: Differentiate the conductor's potential
steps: Inside r<R the potential is constant, so E=0.
Outside, V=kQ/r, so
E
=k
Q
/r².
The field jumps at the charged surface and then falls to one quarter its surface value at 2R, matching C.
pitfall: The potential is continuous at the surface while its slope, and hence E, can jump.
integration: E_r=−dV/dr; the flat interior and inverse-r exterior must be treated piecewise.

title: Move a charge through a shell's hole
steps: Initial potential is kQ/r; the shell's entire interior is at kQ/R.
External slow-transfer work is q(V_f−V_i).
W_ext=kqQ(1/R−1/r).
pitfall: Do not continue the point-charge formula kQ/r to the shell's center.
integration: Integrate only outside: −q∫rᴿ kQ/s² ds, then add the zero interior integral.

title: Uniform plate field
steps: Neglecting edge effects, E is uniform between the plates.
The voltage magnitude satisfies V₀=Ed.
Therefore E=V₀/d.
pitfall: Disconnecting the battery does not instantly change the existing Q, V, or E.
integration: |ΔV|=|−∫₀ᵈ E dl|=Ed.

title: Merge charged droplets
steps: Conservation gives new charge 2Q and new volume twice the original.
Since volume is proportional to R³, R_new=2^(1/3)R.
pitfall: The radius does not double when volume doubles.
integration: The surface potential follows by integrating the exterior radial field: V_surface=kQ/R.

title: Area under a linear field
steps: ΔV=−∫₀⁰.⁵(40x+4)dx.
An antiderivative is 20x²+4x, so the integral is 5+2=7 V.
pitfall: Using only the final field times distance overestimates a changing field.
integration: The exact alternative is trapezoid area: average field (4+24)/2=14 V/m times 0.5 m gives 7 V, then apply the minus sign.

title: Equal distances reduce to a charge sum
steps: P is equally far from all three vertices, so V=kΣq/r.
Only arrangement E has total charge +3q−q−2q=0.
Thus E gives zero potential at P.
pitfall: Do not demand equal-and-opposite pairs; any zero algebraic sum works at equal distances.
integration: Factor the common 1/r out of the sum of source potential integrals.

title: Average power for a charge transfer
steps: The required rest-to-rest work is qΔV=(4×10⁻⁶)(70−50)=8×10⁻⁵ J.
Average power is work divided by time.
pitfall: Use the 20 V difference, not the final 70 V alone.
integration: W=−q∫E·dl=qΔV; divide the integrated work by the given 5 s.

title: Potential from two positive sources
steps: With zero potential at infinity, each source contributes a positive kq/r at every finite nonsource point.
Their sum cannot be negative anywhere on the line.
Therefore none of the listed spatial ranges has negative potential.
pitfall: A field component may be negative even when potential is positive.
integration: Each potential equals a positive inward field-work integral from infinity for a positive source.

title: Compare two drops in attractive potential
steps: Outside the sphere, U(r)=−kQq/r.
From 2d to d the kinetic-energy gain is kQq/(2d)=K₀.
From 4d to d the gain is 3kQq/(4d)=(3/2)K₀.
pitfall: The initial separation matters; both trials end at the same point but start with different U.
integration: K=∫r_iᵈ (−kQq/r²)dr=kQq(1/d−1/r_i).

title: Evaluate potential at labeled positions
steps: The sources are +2Q at x=0 and +Q at x=5 m.
In units kQ/m, V at x=1,2,3,4,6 is respectively 2.25, 1.333, 1.167, 1.5, and 1.333.
The largest is at 1 m, option A.
pitfall: Comparing only nearest-source distances misses the unequal source charges.
integration: Add the two signed scalar source integrals kq/r at each point.

title: Count zero-potential points
steps: Let −5 μC be at x=0 and +10 μC at x=0.5 m.
V=0 requires distance to +10 μC to be twice the distance to −5 μC.
One solution lies between the charges at x=1/6 m; another lies to the left at x=−0.5 m. There are two finite solutions.
pitfall: Do not look only between the charges; use absolute distances in all three intervals.
integration: The two source potential integrals cancel where −5/|x|+10/|x−0.5|=0.

title: Integrate a linearly varying negative field
steps: VB−VA=−∫₂⁷(−75x)dx.
B is higher by about 1690 V, option E.
pitfall: The field points toward decreasing x, so potential rises as x increases.
integration: The antiderivative of 75x is 37.5x²; subtract both endpoint values.

title: Horizontal line integral with a source caveat
steps: Along the horizontal segment y=Y from x=0 to x=X, dy=0.
Thus −∫E·dl=−∫₀ˣ6xY dx=−3X²Y, the intended answer C.
However, the specified full field has ∂Ey/∂x−∂Ex/∂y=−6x≠0, so it is not a conservative electrostatic field and does not define a global path-independent potential as written.
pitfall: The Ey term does no work on this horizontal path; also distinguish a path integral from a valid global potential difference.
integration: Explicitly parameterize the segment (x,Y), substitute dl=(dx,0), and integrate x. The inconsistency in the source does not change this segment's integral.

title: Distances of four and five meters
steps: The −4 nC charge is at the origin and +10 nC is at (3,0); P is (0,4).
Their distances from P are 4 m and 5 m.
pitfall: The diagonal source-to-P distance is 5 m, not 3 m.
integration: Add the two potential integrals kq/r after using the 3–4–5 geometry.

title: Differentiate an inverse-square potential
steps: V=ar⁻², so dV/dr=−2ar⁻³.
The radial field is E_r=−dV/dr=+2ar⁻³.
Choose E.
pitfall: The minus sign in E=−∇V cancels the derivative's negative exponent factor.
integration: Integrating −2ar⁻³ with respect to r reproduces ar⁻² plus a constant.

title: Field magnitude from a radial quadratic
steps: The source gives V(r)=kr².
E_r=−dV/dr=−2kr, pointing inward for k>0.
At r₀ the magnitude is 2kr₀.
pitfall: The requested magnitude is positive even though the radial component is negative.
integration: Differentiating the radial potential is equivalent to inverting ΔV=−∫E_r dr.

title: Compare positive and negative contributions
steps: Among A, B, and C, the distance to the negative sphere is equal, while C is closer to the positive sources, so C has the largest of those three potentials.
C and D are equally distant from both positive spheres by symmetry, but D is farther from the negative sphere; hence VD>VC.

D and E are equally far from sphere 2; D's additional positive contribution from sphere 1 exceeds its negative contribution from sphere 3, whereas at E those two contributions are equal and cancel. Thus D is highest.
pitfall: Compare signed sums; the closest point to a negative charge is not a potential maximum.
integration: Use V=kΣq/r, obtained from the sum of source field integrals, and compare terms whose distances are equal before calculating anything.

title: Potential difference is work per charge
steps: For the intended slow/rest-to-rest move, W_ext=qΔV.
Choose 2.5×10³ V.
pitfall: The distance 3 m is not needed when work and charge are supplied.
integration: W_ext=−q∫E·dl, so divide the work integral by q to obtain ΔV.

title: Bring a seventh charge to a symmetric center
steps: Each of the six fixed charges contributes kQ/R at the center.
The existing potential there is 6kQ/R.
The added charge +Q requires work QV=6kQ²/R=3Q²/(2πε₀R), option D.
pitfall: Do not recalculate the unchanged interactions among the six fixed charges.
integration: Only the incoming charge's work integral is new: W_ext=−Q∫∞ᶜ E_existing·dl=QV_center.

title: Field work for an upward displacement
steps: A→B rises by 5 sin37°≈3 m, while the field is downward.
W_field=qE·Δr=−e(1000)(3).
The work is −3000 eV.
pitfall: Use the vertical component, and distinguish field work from potential-energy change.
integration: W=e∫E_y dy=e∫(−1000)dy; horizontal motion contributes zero.

title: Work to a square's center
steps: Each of four corner charges is L/√2 from the center.
V_center=4kQ/(L/√2)=4√2kQ/L.
Bringing +Q from infinity requires W_ext=QV=4√2kQ²/L.
pitfall: The field cancels exactly at the endpoint, but work to reach that endpoint is not zero.
integration: Integrate the existing net field along the incoming path; the result is −QΔV for field work, opposite for slow external work.

title: Make the center potential vanish
steps: All corners are the same distance from A.
The existing charge sum is 3Q; zero potential requires total charge sum zero.
The missing charge must be −3Q.
pitfall: A charge −Q cancels only one of the three equal positive contributions.
integration: At equal source distances, V=(k/r)Σq, the discrete version of ∫k dq/r.

title: Potential energy in an upward field
steps: The proton moves upward by Δy=5 sin37°≈3 m.
ΔV=−EΔy=−3000 V.
ΔU=eΔV=−3000 eV, option B.
pitfall: Here the field points up, opposite to the diagram in question 77; read each problem's direction independently.
integration: ΔU=−e∫Aᴮ E·dl=−e∫E_y dy.

title: Compare changes in speed squared
steps: The required electric energy is proportional to v_f²−v_i².
First change: (2v₀)²−v₀²=3v₀². Second: (4v₀)²−(2v₀)²=12v₀².
The second potential difference is four times the first.
pitfall: Compare changes in kinetic energy, not changes in speed.
integration: −q∫dV=∫mv dv=(m/2)(v_f²−v_i²); both integrals scale by four.

title: Move a positive charge inward
steps: The positive sphere's field points outward; the imposed motion is inward.
The field does negative work, so ΔU>0.
Indeed V(0)=3kQ/(2Rₛ) and V(2Rₛ)=kQ/(2Rₛ), giving ΔU=kQq/Rₛ>0.
pitfall: E=0 at the center does not imply V=0 or ΔU=0.
integration: Split −q∫E dr at Rₛ: use kQ/r² outside and kQr/Rₛ³ inside.

title: Integrate a nonuniform field
steps: ΔV=−∫₀.₂⁰ 1200x² dx=+3.2 V.
An electron has q=−e, so ΔU=qΔV=−3.2 eV.
The electron loses potential energy as it moves opposite the field.
pitfall: Do not use E at one endpoint times the full displacement.
integration: The antiderivative is 400x³; reverse limits give a negative field integral, then the leading minus sign makes ΔV positive.

title: Only endpoints determine energy change
steps: Read P=10 V, Q=20 V, R=30 V, S=20 V, T=40 V.
For a positive charge, the four net changes are q(20 V), 0, q(10 V), and q(−10 V).
The largest increase is P→Q→R.
pitfall: Adding absolute changes along a route would incorrectly count temporary increases twice.
integration: The line integral telescopes: −q∫P^Q E·dl−q∫Q^R E·dl=q(VR−VP).

title: A negative charge going to higher potential
steps: The potential change is +10−(−10)=+20 V.
ΔU=qΔV is negative because q<0.
The direction of motion staying the same does not determine the energy change.
pitfall: Potential and potential energy have opposite trends for a negative charge.
integration: ΔU=−q∫E·dl=qΔV; the sign of q must remain in the expression.

title: Ratio of two energy changes
steps: For a proton ΔU=e(V_f−V_i).
The changes are −300eV and −400eV.
Their ratio is 400/300=4/3.
pitfall: Use final minus initial before taking the ratio.
integration: Both changes equal −e times the line integral of E; the endpoint voltage differences give the integrals directly.

title: A proton slows as it climbs potential
steps: With only electric work, K+qV is conserved.
The proton's kinetic energy decreases, so its potential energy increases.
Since q>0, V₂>V₁.
pitfall: The force opposes the velocity when the particle slows.
integration: ∫F·dx=ΔK<0; therefore ΔV=−ΔK/e>0.

title: Work outside a spherical shell
steps: The initial distance from the center is 2R; final potential anywhere inside the shell is kQ/R.
W_ext=q[kQ/R−kQ/(2R)]=kQq/(2R)>0 for slow transport.
There is no additional work inside because E=0 there.
pitfall: The zero interior field does not cancel the work outside.
integration: W_ext=−q∫₂ᴿᴿ kQ/r² dr−q∫ᴿ⁰0dr=kQq/(2R).

title: Energy sharing between unequal masses
steps: Initially all energy is positive U=kq²/d. Far apart U approaches zero, so K₁+K₂ equals that initial energy.
Total momentum remains zero: both spheres have equal momentum magnitudes.
K=p²/(2m), so the lighter sphere 1 has greater kinetic energy. Chart D satisfies both conditions.
pitfall: Equal forces do not give equal kinetic energies when masses differ.
integration: Integrating each F·dr gives its kinetic energy; momentum conservation determines how the total released U is divided.

title: Speed gained by attraction
steps: At infinity both K and U are approximately zero.
v=√(2K/m)=√60≈7.75 m/s, closest to 8 m/s.
pitfall: Convert millimeters to meters before calculating.
integration: K=∫∞ʳ F_r dr with F_r=−k|Qq|/r², giving k|Qq|/r.

title: Same charge and voltage give same energy
steps: The magnitude of potential-energy change is
qΔV
for either particle.
Both start from rest, so their final kinetic energies equal that same released energy.
Mass changes the final speed, not the energy gain here.
pitfall: A heavier particle need not have greater kinetic energy.
integration: W=q∫E·dl=−qΔV is independent of mass.

title: Speed scales as square root of voltage
steps: From rest, (1/2)mv²=
eΔV
Quadrupling the voltage quadruples kinetic energy.
The speed doubles: v₂/v₁=2.
pitfall: A factor of four in energy gives a factor of two in speed.
integration: ∫mv dv=−e∫dV leads directly to v² proportional to voltage magnitude.

title: Keep the initial kinetic energy
steps: The potential change is −ΔV, so a +e ion gains kinetic energy eΔV.
Set (1/2)mv_f²=(1/2)mv₀²+eΔV.
v_f=√(v₀²+2eΔV/m).
pitfall: The expression √(2eΔV/m) applies only when the initial speed is zero.
integration: Integrate mv dv from v₀ to v_f and −e dV over the stated potential drop.

title: Energy through two successive fields
steps: The source supplies kinetic energy eV₀.
In the second region the ion descends d/2 in field V₀/d, gaining another eV₀/2.
Thus K_P=3eV₀/2 and v_P=√(3eV₀/M).
pitfall: Horizontal travel in the second region contributes no electric work.
integration: The second work integral is e∫₀ᵈ⧸² (V₀/d)dy=eV₀/2; only displacement parallel to E contributes.

title: An escaping negative charge slows
steps: For unlike charges U=−k
Qq
As separation grows, U becomes less negative: U₂>U₁.
Conservation of energy then gives K₂<K₁.
pitfall: A less negative potential energy is a larger potential energy.
integration: The attractive force is opposite outward motion, so ∫F·dr<0 and ΔK<0.

title: Find the reachable turning point
steps: At x=0 the V graph slopes downward, so E=−dV/dx points right.
A negative charge initially accelerates left. Its next rest point must have V(x)=V(0) because K+qV is constant.
The reachable equal-potential point is xA, not xD on the other side of an inaccessible lower-V region.
pitfall: For a negative charge, lower V corresponds to higher U; the particle cannot cross the right-hand potential-energy barrier from rest.
integration: K(x)=−q[V(x)−V(0)]; allowed motion requires K≥0. For q<0 this requires V(x)≥V(0).

title: Evaluate each kinetic-energy gain
steps: The distances are P:r/2, R:r, S:2r. Let A=kQq/r.
Charge 1 gains A; charge 2 gains 2A.
Charge 3 has −2q and falls from 2r to r, gaining A. Hence K₂>K₁=K₃.
pitfall: The different mass affects speed but not qΔV.
integration: For each trial K=−q_test∫dV=q_test kQ(1/r_i−1/r_f), with its own signed q_test.

title: Compare gains at two final radii
steps: For repulsion from rest at d, K(r)=kQq(1/d−1/r).
At 2d the gain is kQq/(2d); at 3d it is 2kQq/(3d).
The ratio KX/KY=(1/2)/(2/3)=3/4.
pitfall: The energy ratio is not simply the ratio of final distances.
integration: Integrate the force: K(r)=∫dʳ kQq/s² ds=kQq(1/d−1/r).

title: An electron accelerates downward
steps: Because q<0, its force is opposite the upward field.
It speeds up, so kinetic energy increases.
With only electric work, the electron-field potential energy decreases.
pitfall: The electron moves downward; a claim that it moves upward has the wrong force direction.
integration: ΔK=q∫E·dl>0 because both q and E·dl are negative; ΔU=−ΔK.

title: Scale charge, field, and distance
steps: From rest, (1/2)mv²=qED for motion along the force.
The second energy is (1/2 Q₁)(2E₁)(2D₁)=2Q₁E₁D₁.
Equal masses imply v₂=√2 v₁.
pitfall: The energy doubles, not the speed.
integration: For a uniform field ∫qE ds=qED; use the product of all three scale factors before taking the square root.

title: Reverse and double one charge
steps: External rest-to-rest work is ΔU, proportional to the product of the two charges.
Replacing −Q by +2Q multiplies that product, and therefore the work, by −2.
The new work is −2W. The old W was negative and the new work is positive.
pitfall: Keep the sign of the original W.
integration: The entire integral W_ext=−∫F_electric·dl is linear in the moving charge, so it acquires the factor −2.

title: Potential inside a charged metal sphere
steps: A conductor contains mobile electrons. In electrostatic equilibrium they have redistributed until the electric field in the metal is zero.
The potential at the surface, using zero potential at infinity, is V(R)=kQ/R, where k=1/(4πε₀).
Zero field means no change in potential as you travel from the surface to the center. Therefore V(0)=kQ/R.
pitfall: Zero electric field means constant potential, not necessarily zero potential.
integration: V(0)−V(R)=−∫ from R to 0 E(r)dr=0. First obtain V(R)=−∫ from ∞ to R kQ/r² dr=kQ/R.

title: Charge on an isolated metal box
steps: Draw a closed Gaussian surface inside the metal, surrounding its cavity. The electric field on that surface is zero.
Gauss’s law then requires Q+q_inner=0, so the inside wall carries −Q.
The box itself began neutral and is not grounded. Its total charge remains zero, so q_outer=+Q.
A nonspherical box need not produce the same exterior field as a bare point charge.
pitfall: Do not confuse the empty cavity with the metal material: the field in the cavity is generally nonzero.
integration: ∮ E·dA=0=(Q+q_inner)/ε₀. This closed-surface integral fixes the total inner charge without finding its detailed distribution.

title: Charging two spheres by induction
steps: The negative rod repels mobile electrons away from sphere X.
While X and Y touch, electrons can move from X onto Y.
Separate Y while the rod is still present: Y keeps excess electrons and is negative; X has lost electrons and is positive.
Removing the rod only lets each sphere’s remaining charge spread over its own surface.
pitfall: No contact with the rod is needed. Total charge of X and Y remains zero.
integration: Integration is unnecessary: track electron motion and conserve the total charge.

title: The field must be normal to a conductor
steps: The question asks for the incorrect statement.
At equilibrium the metal is an equipotential and the electric field inside it is zero.
A nonzero tangential field at the surface would push mobile charges along that surface, contradicting equilibrium.
Thus the external field is perpendicular, not parallel, to the surface: D is false.
pitfall: An EXCEPT question asks you to select the false statement.
integration: Along a surface path, ΔV=−∫E·dl=0. Locally this requires the tangential component of E to vanish.

title: Uneven surface charge, one potential
steps: The rod polarizes the metal: electrons gather farther from the rod, leaving the near side positive.
Charges continue moving whenever there is a potential difference within the connected metal.
Once motion stops, every point on and inside the conductor has the same electric potential, despite its different local charge densities.
pitfall: Positive and negative patches on one conductor do not imply different equilibrium potentials.
integration: For any path within the metal, V_B−V_A=−∫A→B E·dl=0 because E=0.

title: Field of an isolated hollow charged sphere
steps: Spherical symmetry makes the exterior field radial. For a positive total charge it points outward, so I is true.
Outside, Gauss’s law gives E=kQ/r², which is not zero; II is false.
Inside the empty spherical cavity and inside the metal, E=0; III is true.
The correct combination is I and III.
pitfall: The zero-field rule inside does not extend to the space outside the sphere.
integration: A concentric sphere outside gives E(4πr²)=Q/ε₀; a concentric sphere inside the empty cavity encloses no charge and symmetry gives E=0.

title: Volume charge identifies an insulator
steps: The phrase “uniformly throughout” describes a nonzero volume charge density.
If this were a metal at electrostatic equilibrium, its excess charge would migrate to its surface.
Therefore the charged solid is not metal. An insulating solid can retain charge distributed through its volume.
pitfall: A uniformly charged solid insulator and a conducting sphere have different internal fields.
integration: For the insulating sphere, Q_enc(r)=∫₀ʳρ4πs²ds=4πρr³/3, so E=ρr/(3ε₀), generally nonzero.

title: Distinguish electric field from potential
steps: Free charges in the conducting sphere rearrange until E=0 throughout its interior.
With V(∞)=0, the surface potential is kQ/R.
The interior shares this constant positive potential. Thus E=0 and V≠0.
pitfall: Potential depends on a reference; the conventional reference here is infinity.
integration: Integrate from infinity to the surface to get kQ/R; the additional integral through the interior is zero.

title: Metal versus charged cavity
steps: Point X lies in the cavity containing +Q; this is empty space, not conducting material, so its field need not vanish.
Point Y lies in the solid metal. Electrostatic equilibrium guarantees E_Y=0.
Point Z is outside. The induced outer charge produces an external field; it is not a shielded interior point.
Only Y has zero field.
pitfall: A cavity containing a charge is not field-free, even though the surrounding metal is.
integration: A Gaussian surface inside the metal has ∮E·dA=0, forcing inner charge −Q; the neutral metal then has +Q on its outer surface.

title: Two concentric conducting shells
steps: The inner shell contributes a total +10 nC inside a Gaussian surface drawn through the outer shell’s metal.
To make the field zero there, the inner face of the outer shell must carry −10 nC.
The entire outer shell has −20 nC, so its outer face carries −20−(−10)=−10 nC.
pitfall: The −20 nC is the total charge of the outer shell, not the charge on either one of its faces.
integration: 0=∮E·dA=(10 nC+q_inner)/ε₀, then use q_inner+q_outer=−20 nC.

title: Changing the shape of a conductor
steps: Both shapes remain conductors in equilibrium: all excess charge is on the outer surface, the interior field is zero, and the potential is constant.
The spherical object has the same curvature everywhere and, without external influences, uniform surface charge density.
The irregular shape has different curvatures. Surface charge density and the field just outside therefore vary from point to point.
Only statement E describes the change.
pitfall: An equipotential surface can have different electric-field magnitudes at different points.
integration: A tiny Gaussian pillbox gives E_normal=σ/ε₀. Unequal σ produces unequal E while the tangential potential integral stays zero.

title: Induced charge fixed by zero flux
steps: The central sphere carries −5 nC.
A closed surface entirely in the surrounding metal has zero electric flux, so its enclosed total charge must be zero.
The shell’s inside wall must therefore have +5 nC; its outside wall has the remaining +9−5=+4 nC.
This cancellation requirement, not equal area or quantization, explains the unequal amounts.
pitfall: A conductor need not have the same surface charge density on its inner and outer faces.
integration: ∮E·dA=0=(−5 nC+q_inner)/ε₀.

title: A positive charge polarizes a positive sphere
steps: The external positive charge is on the left. It attracts the sphere’s electrons toward the left side.
The right side loses electrons and becomes more positively charged.
The sphere’s total charge remains +Q because it is isolated. Its distribution is not uniform, and the right half has net positive charge.
pitfall: The sphere can redistribute charge without changing its total charge.
integration: No integral is needed to choose the sign. Computing the full surface distribution would require a more advanced boundary-value solution.

title: Connected spheres share potential
steps: The nearby positive rod attracts electrons toward sphere 1.
Electrons can arrive through the wire from sphere 2, leaving sphere 1 negative and sphere 2 positive.
The spheres and wire form one connected conductor. When equilibrium is reached their potentials must be equal.
pitfall: Equal potential does not require equal net charge or even the same sign of charge when an external source is present.
integration: The voltage difference along the conducting connection is −∫E·dl=0 at equilibrium.

title: Polarized sphere remains equipotential
steps: The positive rod attracts electrons to the nearer part of the neutral sphere.
This redistribution creates a field that cancels the applied field inside the metal.
Every point on the conductor, including points 1 and 2, has the same potential. The valid reason is the conductor’s equilibrium condition.
pitfall: Neutral matter still contains many positive and negative charges; neutrality does not mean no charges exist.
integration: V₂−V₁=−∫₁² E·dl=0 along a path inside the metal.

title: A pillbox crossing a conductor surface
steps: Point A is inside the metal, so E_A=0 and the inner end face contributes zero flux.
The outer face lies just beyond positively induced surface charge on the disk’s right face.
The thin pillbox encloses nonzero charge. Gauss’s law therefore requires nonzero outward flux through its outer face.
This is why the field at B is nonzero.
pitfall: Zero field in the metal does not imply zero field immediately outside it.
integration: In the thin-pillbox limit the side flux vanishes: E_B A=σ₂A/ε₀, so E_B=σ₂/ε₀.

title: The two faces of a polarized disk
steps: The external positive particle lies to the left of the initially neutral disk.
Electrons move toward it and accumulate on the left face, giving σ₁<0.
The right face has an electron deficit, giving σ₂>0. The total disk charge remains zero.
pitfall: An isolated neutral conductor can have nonzero charge on both faces with opposite signs.
integration: Integrating σ over all disk surfaces gives ∫σdA=0; this total-charge constraint does not mean σ is zero at each point.

title: Potential halfway inside a conductor
steps: The conductor’s surface potential is kQ/r.
The field is zero at every radius inside it, so the potential is constant throughout.
At radius r/2 the potential is still kQ/r, giving C.
pitfall: Do not substitute r/2 into kQ/d: that point-charge formula is valid outside this sphere, not inside its metal.

title: Charge concentrates at the sharp outer tip
steps: The cavity contains no charge, so there is no induced charge on its inner wall. Points B and C do not hold the object’s excess charge.
All added negative charge resides on the external surface.
Point A is the sharper outer tip, with smaller radius of curvature than point D. Its surface charge density has the greatest magnitude.
pitfall: The sharp edge of an empty internal cavity is not where the excess charge accumulates.
integration: Gauss’s law in the metal encloses no cavity charge, and a surface pillbox relates the external field to σ by E_normal=σ/ε₀.

title: Curvature changes field, not potential
steps: X, Y, and Z belong to the same connected metal object.
If their potentials differed, mobile electrons would move, contradicting the assumed equilibrium.
Therefore V_X=V_Y=V_Z. Their different curvatures affect local surface charge density and field, not this equality.
pitfall: Do not rank voltage using tip sharpness.
integration: The line integral of E between any two points through the metal is zero, so their potential difference is zero.

title: A metal slab between charged plates
steps: Charge induced on the two slab faces cancels the plate field inside the metal, so E₂=0.
In the ideal large-plate approximation, each vacuum gap has the same field magnitude σ/ε₀ set by the plate charge.
Thus E₁=E₃>E₂.
pitfall: Inserting metal does not make the electric field vanish everywhere between the original plates.
integration: Treat the path as three intervals. The voltage drop is −∫gap1 E dl−∫metal 0 dl−∫gap3 E dl; only the gaps contribute.

title: External charge and surface potential
steps: The external +Q charge induces negative charge on the near side and positive charge on the far side.
The induced field ensures no tangential field remains on the sphere’s surface.
The total potential, including the external charge and the sphere’s induced charges, is the same at points 1, 2, and 3.
pitfall: Using kQ/d for the external particle alone ignores the induced surface charges.
integration: The total field satisfies V_j−V_i=−∫i→j E_total·dl=0 along the conducting surface.

title: Stronger applied field, same metal interior
steps: In either case mobile charges on the sphere rearrange in response to the external plates.
Equilibrium requires E=0 inside the conducting material, regardless of how large the applied static field is within the ideal model.
Thus E₁=E₂=0, so the intended answer is B.
pitfall: The comparison is between two zero fields. The phrase “double the field” is not the physical description of the interior response.
integration: Any potential difference inside is −∫E·dl=0 in both cases.

title: Polarization without charging
steps: The negative rod is near the sphere’s left side and repels electrons toward the right.
The left side becomes positively charged and the right side negatively charged.
There is neither contact nor a ground connection, so the sphere keeps zero net charge.
pitfall: Polarization changes where charge sits; charging changes the total amount.
integration: Charge conservation is sufficient: ∫surface σdA=0 even though σ varies across the surface.

title: Equilibrium inside charged metal
steps: A nonzero internal field would accelerate mobile charges, so the equilibrium interior field must be zero.
Zero field means potential is uniform inside.
For an isolated charged sphere with zero potential at infinity, that uniform value is kQ/R and is nonzero.
pitfall: The derivative of a constant potential is zero even when the constant itself is nonzero.
integration: E_r=−dV/dr=0 implies V is constant; the boundary value V(R)=kQ/R fixes that constant.

title: Field strongest at the smaller curved end
steps: The illustrated end X has smaller radius of curvature than Y.
On this isolated charged conductor, charge concentrates more strongly near the sharper end.
The local relation E_normal=σ/ε₀ makes the field magnitude just outside X greater than at Y.
pitfall: The conclusion concerns the local field, not a higher potential at the tip.
integration: A Gaussian pillbox straddling each surface gives E_X=σ_X/ε₀ and E_Y=σ_Y/ε₀. The sharper X end has larger σ.

title: One conductor, one nonzero potential
steps: X and Y are points on a single connected conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
The tangential field vanishes, so the potential is the same at both ends.
The isolated conductor is positively charged and V(∞)=0, so this common potential is nonzero.
pitfall: The fact that E_X>E_Y from the preceding question does not imply V_X>V_Y.
integration: V_Y−V_X=−∫X→Y E·dl=0 along a surface or internal conducting path.

title: Electric field just inside a metal plate
steps: The wording asks for the field inside the conducting plate, just beneath its surface.
At electrostatic equilibrium the interior electric field of a conductor is zero.
Therefore the answer is A. The formulas proportional to Q/A describe fields outside, under suitable ideal-plate assumptions.
pitfall: Read “inside” carefully. Immediately outside an isolated broad plate the field can be Q/(2ε₀A), but that is a different location.
integration: A pillbox boundary condition is E_out−E_in=σ/ε₀; with E_in=0 this determines E_out, not a nonzero E_in.

title: Direction near a negatively charged surface
steps: The field immediately outside a conductor must be perpendicular to its surface.
At P the cylindrical side is horizontal, so the perpendicular direction is vertical.
The surface is negatively charged, so field lines point inward toward it. The downward arrow in C is correct.
pitfall: A diagonal arrow would have a tangential component and could not represent electrostatic equilibrium.
integration: Along the surface dV=−E·dl=0, forcing E_tangent=0; the sign of σ fixes the normal direction.

title: Separate conductors while the rod remains
steps: The negative rod near conductor 1 repels electrons through the contact toward conductor 2.
Conductor 2 gains electrons while conductor 1 loses them.
Separating the conductors with the rod still present traps this excess on conductor 2. It is negatively charged.
pitfall: The rod never touches the conductors, but their mutual contact supplies an electron-transfer path.
integration: An integral is unnecessary; use conservation of charge and the sign of the electron’s force.

title: Inner wall of a charged conducting shell
steps: Take a Gaussian surface through the metal wall, around the central +Q.
The field throughout the metal is zero, requiring zero net enclosed charge.
Therefore the inner surface carries −Q. The shell’s remaining +6Q is on its outside, keeping its total +5Q.
pitfall: It is the zero electric field, not zero electric potential, that justifies the inner charge.
integration: 0=∮E·dA=(Q+q_inner)/ε₀ gives q_inner=−Q.

title: Induction on the inner face of the outer shell
steps: The enclosed inner sphere carries −Q.
A Gaussian surface within the outer conducting shell must enclose zero net charge.
The outer shell’s inner face therefore carries +Q.
pitfall: The shell’s total +3Q does not all go to its inner face.
integration: 0=∮E·dA=(−Q+q_inner)/ε₀, so q_inner=+Q.

title: Remaining charge on the outer face
steps: The outer shell has total charge +3Q.
Its inner face must carry +Q to cancel the enclosed inner sphere’s −Q in a Gaussian surface through the metal.
The remaining charge on the outer face is +3Q−Q=+2Q.
pitfall: Always distinguish “charge of the shell” from “charge on one shell surface.”
integration: Combine the zero-flux result q_inner=+Q with ∫all surfaces σdA=3Q.

title: How a conductor reaches equilibrium
steps: A neutral metal still contains mobile electrons.
Immediately after it is placed in the external field, the field exerts forces on those electrons and redistributes them.
The induced charge creates a compensating field. Motion stops when the interior field is zero and the surface is again equipotential.
This transient redistribution is described by A.
pitfall: Neutral does not mean unaffected by an electric field.
integration: During the transient, ∫E·dl can be nonzero. At final electrostatic equilibrium, all internal voltage differences vanish.

title: Electrostatic shielding of a cavity
steps: The external charges polarize the shell’s outside surface, but a closed conductor shields the cavity from their electrostatic fields.
The +Q shown at the center produces a uniform −Q distribution on the spherical cavity wall. That spherical wall contributes zero field in the cavity.
At P the field is therefore due to Q alone, E=kQ/r², with r measured from Q to P. External charge magnitudes do not enter.
pitfall: Shielding removes external influences; it does not remove the field of a charge placed inside the cavity.
integration: A concentric Gaussian sphere within the cavity gives E(4πr²)=Q/ε₀ for the centered charge shown.

title: Work along two equipotential paths
steps: Both endpoints are on the same equipotential conducting sphere.
Along the path through the metal E=0, so electric work is zero.
Along the surface the field has no tangential component, so electric work is again zero.
Thus W_S=W_C=0, and E supplies the correct justification.
pitfall: Same displacement is not the general reason electric work is path independent; electrostatic fields are conservative.
integration: W_field=q∫A→B E·dl=0 for either route; quasistatic external work qΔV is also zero.

title: What connected metal spheres equalize
steps: While the wire connects them, the two spheres form one conductor.
Charge flows until their electric potentials are equal: kq₁/r₁=kq₂/r₂ in the well-separated approximation.
Thus q₁/q₂=r₁/r₂. Different radii generally mean different charges, capacitances, and surface fields, but equal voltage.
pitfall: Charge does not necessarily split equally between spheres of different sizes.
integration: V(r)=−∫∞ʳ kq/s² ds=kq/r. Equating these integrated potentials gives the charge ratio.

title: Charge sharing with radii r and 2r
steps: The total initial charge is 2Q, not Q.
Equal final potentials imply q_X/r=q_Y/(2r), hence q_Y=2q_X.
Conservation gives q_X+q_Y=3q_X=2Q. Therefore q_X=2Q/3.
pitfall: Use total charge 2Q because both spheres initially carry Q.
integration: Integrate each exterior field to obtain V_X=kq_X/r and V_Y=kq_Y/(2r), then set V_X=V_Y.

title: Voltage ratio after the wire is removed
steps: The wire allows charges to move until V_X=V_Y.
Removing it after current has stopped preserves the sphere charges in the stated fixed, well-separated geometry.
The ratio V_X/V_Y is therefore 1.
pitfall: The larger sphere carries more charge precisely so it can share the same potential.
integration: V_X/V_Y=(∫ᵣ∞ E_X ds)/(∫₂ᵣ∞ E_Y ds)=1 after equalization.

title: Remove the rod before removing ground
steps: With the positive rod near a grounded sphere, electrons are drawn from Earth onto the sphere.
The rod is then moved away while the ground path remains connected. The extra electrons can return to Earth.
Only after neutrality has been restored is the ground disconnected. The sphere ends neutral and unpolarized.
pitfall: The order matters: disconnecting ground first would instead trap negative charge.
integration: No integration is necessary; track the available electron path at each stage.

title: A negative rod leaves a positive sphere
steps: The negative rod repels mobile electrons.
While the sphere is grounded, some electrons leave it for Earth.
Disconnecting ground first prevents those electrons from returning. Removing the rod then leaves a net positive sphere.
pitfall: In an ordinary metal wire the moving charges are electrons, not protons.
integration: This is a charge-conservation and sequence problem, so an integral adds no useful simplification.

title: Charge fraction on the smaller sphere
steps: Let the smaller sphere’s final charge be q; the larger sphere then has Q₀−q.
Equal potentials give k(Q₀−q)/R=kq/r.
Use R=ar: Q₀−q=aq, so q=Q₀/(a+1).
The requested fraction is 1/(a+1).
pitfall: The smaller sphere gets the smaller fraction when a>1.
integration: Potential is the integral of the exterior radial field: V_R=k(Q₀−q)/R and V_r=kq/r. Equality yields the same equation.

title: Grounding near a positive particle
steps: The nearby +Q attracts electrons toward the conductor.
The ground wire provides an external reservoir from which electrons can enter.
The conductor therefore acquires net negative charge while the positive particle remains nearby.
pitfall: A grounded conductor is held at Earth’s potential; it is not necessarily neutral.
integration: An integral is not needed for the sign; the boundary condition is V_conductor=V_ground, rather than Q_conductor=0.

title: Two contacting plates become one conductor
steps: When the top and middle plates touch, they form a single conductor of net charge +q.
In the ideal parallel-plate approximation, the nearby bottom plate of charge −q draws the positive surface charge onto the facing underside of the middle plate.
No excess charge remains at the buried contact surface. The net +q is on the bottom face of the combined upper conductor.
pitfall: Charges reside on exposed conductor surfaces, not uniformly through the metal or at a metal–metal internal boundary.
integration: Gauss’s law plus E=0 inside each conductor gives ±q on facing surfaces and zero external field when edge effects are neglected.

title: Equal charge density is not equal voltage
steps: Initially Q=σ4πr² on each sphere.
Substitute into V=kQ/r: V=4πkσr=σr/ε₀. With equal σ, the larger sphere B starts at higher potential.
Electrons, being negative, move from lower potential A toward higher potential B. A states both this direction and its electrical cause.
pitfall: Do not assume electrons move from high potential to low potential; that is the direction of positive-charge motion.
integration: V(r)=∫ᵣ∞ E(s)ds=kQ/r. Replacing Q with σ4πr² reveals V∝r.

title: Charge and voltage for radii R and 3R
steps: Total charge is Q.
At equilibrium q₁/R=q₂/(3R), so q₂=3q₁.
Thus q₁=Q/4 and q₂=3Q/4, while V₁=V₂.
The table row expressing q₁<q₂ and equal potentials is C.
pitfall: Larger charge does not necessarily mean larger potential when the radii differ.
integration: Integrating the radial field gives V_i=kq_i/R_i, which makes equal voltage compatible with a 1:3 charge split.

title: Common potential after sharing
steps: The two radii are R and 2R, so equal potential requires q_large=2q_small.
Total charge Q₀ gives q_small=Q₀/3.
The smaller sphere has V=k(Q₀/3)/R=Q₀/(12πε₀R), choice B.
pitfall: The denominator 3 comes from charge sharing; the factor 4π comes from k.
integration: V_small=∫ᴿ∞ k(Q₀/3)/s² ds=kQ₀/(3R).

title: Electron direction during grounding
steps: The positive rod attracts electrons toward the sphere.
In Step 2 the sphere touches ground, providing a route for electrons to enter.
Negative charge flows from ground to the sphere, which is option C.
pitfall: A final negative charge is caused by an electron surplus, not by positive charges escaping through the ground.
integration: No integral is needed; use the force direction on an electron and the connection to ground.

title: Surface density after unequal spheres share charge
steps: In the standard sphere-sharing model, equal potential gives q₂=2q₁ for radii R and 2R.
Their surface areas are 4πR² and 16πR².
Therefore σ₁/σ₂=(q₁/q₂)(A₂/A₁)=(1/2)×4=2.
This lies in the range σ₂<σ₁<4σ₂, so B is the intended comparison.
pitfall: Equal potential does not mean equal surface charge density; the smaller sphere has the larger density.
integration: Use V_i=∫ᴿⁱ∞ kq_i/s² ds=kq_i/R_i and σ_i=q_i/(4πR_i²). The quiz uses the usual isolated-sphere charge-sharing approximation.

title: Sequential charge sharing among three spheres
steps: Let the small radii be r and the middle radius be R>r. After the first connection, V₁=V₂=2kQ/(R+r).
Sphere 2 then carries 2QR/(R+r). Sphere 3 still carries Q, so its original potential kQ/r is larger than that first common potential.
Connecting 2 to 3 raises their common potential above V₁. Sphere 1 is already isolated and keeps its previous charge.
Thus V₂=V₃>V₁.
pitfall: Sphere 1 is no longer part of the second connection, so it does not share the second equilibrium potential.
integration: The standard well-separated model gives V_final,23=kQ(3R+r)/(R+r)². Subtract V₁ to obtain kQ(R−r)/(R+r)²>0.

title: General two-sphere charge split
steps: Conserve charge: sphere 2 ends with Q−q.
Equal potentials require kq/r₁=k(Q−q)/r₂.
Solve qr₂=Qr₁−qr₁, giving q=Qr₁/(r₁+r₂).
The larger sphere gets more than Q/2, consistent with r₁>r₂.
pitfall: The denominator must include both radii; otherwise charge conservation can fail.
integration: V_i=−∫∞ᴿⁱ E_i(s)ds=kq_i/R_i. Equating the integrals gives the sharing rule.

title: The universal connection rule
steps: The wire joins both spheres into one connected conductor.
A potential difference would continue driving charge through the wire.
At electrostatic equilibrium that difference is zero, so the electric potential is the same on both surfaces.
pitfall: Charge, field magnitude, and charge density generally remain unequal when radii differ.
integration: ΔV=−∫wire E·dl=0 in electrostatic equilibrium.

title: Charge flows away from higher positive voltage
steps: Sphere 2 initially has the higher potential, 1800 V versus 900 V.
On contact, electrons flow toward sphere 2, reducing its net positive charge. Equivalently positive charge is transferred away from sphere 2.
When separated again, its unchanged radius means V₂=kQ₂/R₂ decreases along with Q₂.
Both the charge and potential decrease, giving B.
pitfall: Use the initial voltage difference to predict the direction, not just the initial charge amounts.
integration: For the standard isolated-sphere model, C₁=10 nC/900 V and C₂=8 nC/1800 V. V_f=(18 nC)/(C₁+C₂)≈1157 V and Q₂f≈5.14 nC; both are smaller.

title: Charge ratio follows the radii
steps: At equilibrium the connected spheres must have equal potentials.
kQ_A/R=kQ_B/(R/2) implies Q_A=2Q_B.
Using Q_A+Q_B=Q gives Q_A=2Q/3 and Q_B=Q/3.
Only E pairs these charges with the correct equal-potential explanation.
pitfall: Choice C has the right charges but the wrong explanation: the final surface fields are not equal.
integration: V_A=∫ᴿ∞ kQ_A/r²dr and V_B=∫ᴿ⁄²∞ kQ_B/r²dr. Equating them gives Q_A=2Q_B.

title: Sharing charge between parallel capacitors
steps: Before disconnection, capacitor a stores Q_initial=C_aV₀.
After connection to b, the capacitors are in parallel and share one final voltage V_f.
The isolated connected plates conserve charge: (C_a+C_b)V_f=C_aV₀.
With C_b=3C_a, V_f=V₀/4, which is less than V₀.
pitfall: The battery is disconnected, so voltage is not held fixed. Charge is conserved; stored electrostatic energy need not be.
integration: C=dq/dV is constant for these ideal capacitors, so q=∫₀ⱽ C dV=CV. Adding their charges at common V gives the same result.

title: Switching a charged capacitor onto an empty one
steps: Because C=ε₀A/d, capacitor 1 has C₁=3C₂.
With switch B, only capacitor 2 is charged by the battery, storing Q_initial=C₂ε.
Switch A disconnects the charging path and places the two capacitors in parallel. They settle to the same voltage V_f.
Charge conservation gives (C₁+C₂)V_f=C₂ε, so ΔV₁=ΔV₂=ε/4.
pitfall: Do not assume the battery still fixes the final capacitor voltage after the switch changes position.
integration: For each plate gap, ΔV=−∫E·dl in magnitude is Qd/(ε₀A), giving C=Q/ΔV=ε₀A/d before applying charge conservation.
